en: May my heart— which consists of the emission (*visarga*) of the state vibrating from the union of those two, the Great Mother who is the support of the stainless digit (*vimalakalā*) and the source of the new creation, and the Father whose body is full and whose splendor is hidden within the five faces— throb as the lineage of the supreme nectar. (AbhTs 1.1)
The *Tantrāloka* is so vast that it cannot be fathomed by anyone;
therefore, listen to this *Tantrasāra*, which is composed in straightforward language.
Its obscurity has been dispelled by the light falling from the feet of the sun-like Śrī Śambhunātha.
"Examine this lotus-heart of Abhinavagupta for the sake of worshipping the Great Lord.

Here, knowledge is the cause of liberation because it is the adversary of ignorance, which is the cause of bondage. Ignorance is twofold: residing in the intellect (*buddhi*) and residing in the person (*pauruṣa*). Of these, that residing in the intellect has the nature of non-determination and consists of erroneous determination.

However, we shall explain in the *Malanirṇaya* that the personal [ignorance] (*pauruṣa*) has the nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), consists of contracted manifestation, and is itself the root cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). In that regard, although personal ignorance might be removed through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other means, initiation itself is not possible as long as there exists an ignorance consisting of non-determinative cognition residing in the intellect (*buddhi*), because initiation— consisting of the purification of the principles (*tattva-śuddhi*) and union with Śiva— is preceded by the ascertainment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.

In this regard, knowledge—which consists of ascertainment and resides solely in the intellect—is primary; and when that very [knowledge] is practiced, it destroys even the ignorance pertaining to the person, because the practice of conceptual consciousness culminates in non-conceptual [consciousness]. For the Self, whose nature is Śiva, is of the form of the light of consciousness uncontracted by conceptualization; therefore, knowledge that pertains to all things in every respect and consists of correct certainty must be adopted.
And that [knowledge] is preceded by the study of the scriptures.
And the scripture spoken by the Supreme Lord alone is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),

because the meanings taught in other scriptures are accepted therein with distinction, and because it provides a determination established through reasoning that exceeds those [other] meanings. Therefore, the knowledge taught in other traditions liberates only from a limited portion of bondage, not from all of it.
But the liberating scripture of the Supreme Lord consists of five currents, divided into ten, eighteen, six, and eight parts;
from all of those, the essence is the Trika scriptures (Ṣaḍardhaśāstra); and even more so than those, it is the Mālinīvijaya.
Furthermore, the meaning contained therein cannot be definitively ascertained by mere summary;
nor can there be liberation or the state of being a liberator for one who has not ascertained the true nature of reality, because such a state belongs only to pure knowledge (*jñāna*).
Since the supreme human goal is rooted in well-practiced knowledge, this [treatise] is commenced for its accomplishment.

Ignorance is indeed declared in the scripture to be the cause of bondage; that is known as *mala*. Upon the dawning of even a fraction of perfect knowledge, all of that goes to its very roots. And when the consciousness of the Self arises with every stain destroyed, liberation occurs. Therefore, by means of this scripture, I shall reveal the entirety of the reality of that which is to be known.

In this regard, here, the essential nature (*svabhāva*) alone is the supreme object of attainment. And that [nature] of all entities is nothing other than the form of manifestation (*prakāśa*), for that which is non-manifestation...
Since intrinsic nature is untenable, that [Light] is not manifold; for since it is impossible for Light to admit any other nature, there is no differentiation of its own nature.

Furthermore, space and time are not its differentiators, because they too have the nature of being that very Light. Thus, Light is one alone, and that is indeed consciousness (*saṃvit*), for consciousness is by definition the manifestation of objects; regarding this, there is no dispute among anyone.

And that Light is not dependent; for dependence consists precisely in being an object of manifestation (*prakāśyatā*), and being an object of manifestation necessarily requires another Light. Since there is no other Light whatsoever, Light is one and independent. And because of this very independence, being devoid of limitations by space, time, and form, it is all-pervasive, eternal, and its nature is both with-form and formless in every respect. Its independence is the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), which is its wonder (*camatkāra*).

The power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is the nature of luminosity; the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) is the essence of self-awareness (*āmarśa*); the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is the capacity for all forms; and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is likewise [the capacity for all forms]. Thus, although endowed with these primary powers, in reality that very Light—which is unconditioned, resting in its own bliss, and of the nature of Śiva—is possessed of the powers of will, knowledge, and action. By virtue of its sovereignty, it makes itself contracted.
Illuminating [all things], it is called the "atom" (*aṇu*).
Furthermore, it manifests its own self as independent, by which it shines forth precisely as the nature of Śiva, whose light is undivided.
Even there, by virtue of its sovereignty, it manifests its own self either without means (*anupāya*) or with means (*sopāya*); and even in the case of having means, [it does so].

Whether it be will, knowledge, or action, these are the three means; thus, the threefold nature of immersion (*samāveśa*)—distinguished as *śāmbhava*, *śākta*, and *āṇava*—is taught here in sequence, including its fourfold form as well.
This Self, whose body is light, is Śiva, the autonomous one; by the impetuous play of his own sovereignty, he [reveals] his own essential nature.
That which, having been concealed, is again made manifest in its fullness— either by means of succession and non-succession, or else through the threefold division. Now,
we shall first explain the methodless (anupāya) itself.

When one who has been pierced by a firm descent of power (*śaktipāta*) discerns in this manner all at once, having grasped the word of the Guru, then his immersion (*samāveśa*), which is eternally arisen and devoid of further means, occurs.

If it is asked how he discerns that "here, reasoning (*tarka*) alone is a limb of yoga," it is said in reply: regarding this Supreme Lord, who is one's own Self and whose nature is self-luminous, what could be accomplished by a means? It is not for the sake of attaining His essential nature, because that is eternal; nor is it for the sake of making Him known, because He is ever-manifest.

Because it is self-luminous, there is no removal of an obscuration, since no obscuration whatsoever is possible; nor is there any penetration [of it], because there is no separate entity that could penetrate it. And what means could there be for this, since even such a means is untenable as a separate entity? Therefore, all this is one single reality consisting of pure consciousness alone.

That reality alone—which is unmeasured by time, undivided by space, unfading through limiting adjuncts, unrestricted by forms, unindicated by words, not delineated by means of knowledge, and independent because it assumes its own nature by its own will as the cause for everything from time to the means of knowledge—is a mass of bliss; and that very thing am I. Within that very [reality], within me, the universe is reflected.
For one who thus discerns with firm resolve, the immersion into the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-samāveśa*) occurs perpetually and without any means whatsoever;
nor does it entail any constraint such as mantras, worship, meditation, or ritual conduct. (Abhinavagupta, *Tantrasāra*, Third Chapter)

When one is unable to enter that aforementioned Śiva-principle, which is of the nature of light, within its undivided circle (*akhaṇḍamaṇḍala*), then, perceiving only the supreme power of absolute freedom (*svātantryaśakti*), one experiences the non-conceptual immersion into Bhairava (*nirvikalpa-bhairava-samāveśa*).
And this is his instruction: "All this multitude of phenomena is a mere reflection in the sky of consciousness, because it possesses the defining characteristics of a reflection."
For this is the characteristic of a reflection: that which appears as distinct [from its source] yet is incapable of existing independently, appearing only through its intermingling with another.

It is like a face in a mirror, like taste in saliva, like fragrance in the sense of smell, like the touch of a sexual union in the organ of bliss, like the touch of a spear or a pike in the internal tactile organ, or like an echo in the sky. (AbhTs 3.1)

For that taste is not primary, because its effects, such as the alleviation of disease, are not observed [in that case]. Nor are smell and touch primary qualities of the substratum, because they are impossible in the absence of that [substratum], and because they do not initiate a series of effects.
Yet it is not the case that those two do not exist, since we observe the dusting of the body and the emission [of excrement] and so forth.
Even sound is not primary, for one hears an echo as if it were coming from somewhere, even though no one speaks it.
(AbhTs 3.5) Thus, just as this reflected image appears, so too does the universe appear within the light of the Supreme Lord.
(AbhTs 3.6) But surely, what could the original object (bimba) be here? Let there be none at all. (AbhTs 3.7)
Now, is that [reflection] without a cause? Alas, in that case, there must be an inquiry into its cause. What then?

It will be the very power of the Supreme Lord, synonymous with absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), by means of the metaphorical expression "the original object" (*bimba*). And because He bears the reflection of the universe, the Blessed One possesses the nature of the universe; for the universe consists of consciousness, and it is the locus of the manifestation of pure awareness. Thus it is.
For it is precisely because the universe here is perceived as "this" that He possesses the nature of a reflection;

and yet, this state of being the self of the universe does not remain unapprehended as the essential nature of the Supreme Lord, since it is impossible for that whose very essence is consciousness not to apprehend its own nature.

For if there were no apprehension of one's own nature, there would in reality be insentience; and this apprehension is not merely conventional, but is inseparable from the very fact of having consciousness as its essence.
The *paranādagarbha* has been described; it perceives the entire collection of the powers (*śaktikalāpa*) of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), as far as they constitute the ordering of the universe.
In that regard, there are first of all three primary powers of the Supreme Lord: Anuttara, Icchā, and Unmeṣa; that indeed is it.

The triad of reflective awarenesses—*a*, *i*, and *u*—is derived from this very triad alone; the entire expansion of power (*śaktiprapañca*) is thus carried out. For rest in the Absolute (*anuttara*) is indeed Bliss (*ānanda*); rest in Will (*icchā*) is indeed Sovereignty (*īśana*); and rest in Unfolding (*unmeṣa*) is indeed the Wave (*ūrmi*), which is the very commencement of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). That same triad of reflective awarenesses is *ā*, *ī*, and *ū*. (AbhTs 3.10)

And here, the first three reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*), because their essence consists of the aspect of manifestation (*prakāśa*), are of the nature of the Sun; the final three reflective awarenesses, because they primarily consist of the bliss of the nature of rest (*viśrānti*), are of the nature of the Moon—so long as there is no entry of the factor of action (*karmāṃśa*). But when action enters into Will (*icchā*) and Sovereignty (*īśana*), that which is [thus entered] is called "the desired" (*iṣyamāṇa*) and "the governed" (*īśyamāṇa*).

Then, this [desire] has two divisions: it is called *ra* by its mere manifestation, and *la* by its resting (*viśrānti*). This is because *ra* and *la* have the nature of manifestation and obstruction respectively.
Furthermore, that which is desired is not distinct like an external object; for if it were of a distinct form, it would be a mere emanation (*nirmāṇa*) and not desire or mastery (*īśana*).
Therefore, precisely because of its lack of distinctness, it is merely a sound (*śrutimātra*) of *ra* and *la*, and does not exist as a consonant (*vyañjana*). (AbhTs 3.12)
These four phonemes—ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ—are neuter because they bear the shadow of both [the male and female principles].
(AbhTs 3.13) When there is an expansion of Anuttara and Ānanda within the [powers] beginning with Icchā, then two phonemes arise: e and o.
(AbhTs 3.14) Furthermore, even there, from the union of Anuttara and Ānanda, two phonemes arise: ai and au. (AbhTs 3.15)

This is that power of action (*kriyāśakti*), and it consists of those very four phonemes: *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*. Then again, until everything that has become an effect enters into the Absolute (*anuttara*) at the end of the power of action, it remains as the Bindu (*am*), consisting of pure luminosity by virtue of its essence being consciousness, as previously described.

Then, right there, the emission of the unsurpassed [vowel] arises as *aḥ*. (AbhTs 3.18) Thus, the nature of the seed-syllables of the sixteen self-reflections (*parāmarśa*) is described. (AbhTs 3.19) That which arises from them, consisting of consonants, is the form of the womb (*yoni*). (AbhTs 3.20)

In that regard, from the Anuttara [A] comes the *ka*-group; from faith (*śraddhā*) and desire (*icchā*) comes the *ca*-group; from desire accompanied by action come the two *ṭa*-groups and the *ta*-group; from *unmeṣa* comes the *pa*-group; through union with the five powers (*śakti*), the fivefold nature belongs to desire itself which is threefold; from *unmeṣa* comes the letter *va*; from desire itself which is threefold come *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*; from the emission (*visarga*) comes the letter *ha*; and from the union of the womb (*yoni*) comes the letter *kṣa*.
Thus, this very Blessed One is the Lord of the Kula (*kuleśvara*) in the form of the Anuttara himself.

And for him, there is only one Kauliki power of emission (*visarga-śakti*), by which—from the stage of the nature of bliss onwards, up to this extent that culminates in external creation—the very perceptions of the categories (*varga*) and so forth, as they vibrate, attain the state of being external *tattvas*. And this emission is threefold: the *āṇava*, whose form is the repose of the mind; the *śākta*, characterized by the awakening of the mind; and the *śāmbhava*, whose form is the dissolution of the mind.

Thus, emission (*visarga*) alone is the power of the Lord in the generation of the universe. (AbhTs 3.26) When there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of this much [of the phonemes] as being entirely undivided, then the Lord alone is both the possessor of power (*śaktimān*) and the power (*śakti*), by virtue of his being the seed (*bīja*) and the womb (*yoni*). (AbhTs 3.27) In the reflective awareness of the eight [groups of letters] separately, together with the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvara*), there is a group of nine; when each individual reflective awareness is predominant, there is a nature consisting of fifty [phonemes]. (AbhTs 3.28)
Even there, when considering the possible distinctions of its constituent parts, it consists of eighty-one forms.

However, in reality, there are only six modes of awareness; these become twelve through the process of expansion and reabsorption, thereby nourishing the Supreme Lord’s fullness of universal power (*viśvaśakti*). These very powers, being of the nature of awareness, are defined as the divine Śrī Kālikā.

These pure reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*), which are essentially of the nature of power (*śakti*), assume the form of *vidyā* and *vidyeśvara* within *śuddhavidyā* by virtue of being both supreme and non-supreme (*parāpara*), due to a slight contraction consisting merely in the unfolding of *māyā*. However, within *māyā*, they assume the state of the phonemes of *māyā* (*māyīyavarṇatā*), in which the divisions of duality have become fully manifest. Having reached the state of practical discourse (*vyāvahārikatva*) in *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*, they ultimately attain the nature of external reality. And although these belong to *māyā*, they are like mere bodies [of the higher powers].

When they are perceived, and when their revival is effected by these aforementioned pure reflections which serve as the very life-force, then they become endowed with vitality; and being such, they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, [the state] consists solely of the repose in all reflective awareness, wherein the distinctions of all the principles (*tattva*), elements (*bhūta*), and worlds (*bhuvana*) are reflected.
For one who perceives the Self through non-conceptuality by means of the Śāmbhava immersion, there is liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā).
Here too, as before, there is no constraint whatsoever such as [the use of] mantras and so forth. (AbhTs 3.33–34) — *Tantrasāra*, Fourth Chapter.

In that regard, when one gradually refines conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) for the sake of entering the nature just described, then there is utility for the stages of cultivation (*bhāvanākrama*), which are preceded by sound reasoning, authentic scripture, and the instruction of a true guru.
For it is precisely through the power of conceptual thought that living beings imagine themselves to be bound; that imagination is the cause of obstruction to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, a conceptual thought arising as its opposite shatters the conceptual thought that is the cause of cyclic existence, and thus it is the cause of exalted success (*abhyudaya*).

And that which is of such a nature—transcending all the principles (tattvas) from the limited natures up to Śiva, which consists solely of undivided consciousness—that alone is the ultimate reality (paramārtha), that is the locus for the establishment of things, that is the vital energy (ojaḥ) of the universe; by it the universe breathes, and that alone am I. Therefore, I am both transcendent to the universe and the self of the universe.
"I am [this]"—this [notion] does not arise for those blinded by illusion (*māyā*), due to the absence of right reasoning (*sattarka*) and the other [factors].

For the Vaiṣṇavas and others are restricted by the principle of attachment (*rāgatattva*) to that [lower] level alone according to their scriptures; thus, even when facing the higher vision, they do not turn toward it. Consequently, they are haters of right reasoning, authentic scripture, and the instruction of a true guru.
Thus it is said:
"In the Pārameśvara, it is stated that all those belonging to the Vaiṣṇava and other traditions are colored by attachment to limited knowledge (*vidyā-rāga*);
deprived of the wisdom of the Omniscient One, they do not find the supreme reality. (AbhTs 4.5–4.7)

Therefore, only those pierced by the firm descent of power (*śaktipāta*) from Śambhu enter their supreme essential nature after having purified their conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) through the sequence of the true scriptures and so forth.

Now, one might object: "In this way, the supreme reality would consist of the form of conceptual thought. This is not so; for conceptual thought fulfills its purpose merely by breaking the habitual dwelling in duality, whereas the supreme reality is self-luminous everywhere in all its forms. Thus, [conceptual thought] does not apply there.
Conceptual thought serves neither for the benefit nor for the refutation of anyone.

In that regard, in one who has been pierced by an exceedingly firm descent of power (*śaktipāta*), right reasoning (*sattarka*) arises spontaneously as a result of its innate nature; such a person is said to have been initiated by the Goddesses.
For others, [it arises] through the sequence of the scriptures (*āgama*); we shall explain this in detail in the *Śaktipātaprakāśana*.

However, the function of the teacher is the determination of the scripture (*āgama*); and the function of the scripture is the arising of appropriate conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) which serve as the basis for producing a continuous stream of similar, doubt-free cognitions of that [object].
Such a stream of conceptual constructions is called "right reasoning" (*sattarka*), and it alone is termed "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
It is so called because, although the object is real, it is cultivated by means of this [stream] which brings about its clarity, as if it were unreal due to its previous lack of clarity. (AbhTs 4.12)

And here, apart from right reasoning (*sattarka*) which consists of the light of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), no other limb of yoga is a direct means; for what kind of operation could there be upon consciousness on the part of the group of observances (*niyama*) such as austerity and the like, or the types of restraints (*yama*) such as non-violence and the like, or the group of breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) such as inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth, since these are restricted solely to the object of knowledge (*vedya*)? (AbhTs 4.13)

Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) would likewise render the instruments of perception exceedingly refined; and meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), and absorption (samādhi), being accomplished through the successive stages of practice, would bring about for the meditator identity with the object of meditation.
However, such practice is simply not possible regarding the supreme reality, which is one's own true nature as Śiva.

For practice consists of making the vital breath, intellect, and body subservient to that which is firmly established as consciousness—like the practice of carrying a load, understanding the meaning of a scripture, or learning a dance.
But in the case of the nature of consciousness itself, since there is nothing to be acquired and nothing to be discarded, how can there be practice?
If it is asked, "Is this not also [achieved] through reasoning? it has been stated here that this is merely the method for removing the latent impression of duality, and nothing else at all.

Even in worldly practice, the purpose of cultivation (*abhyāsa*) consists precisely in manifesting the desired form of each respective body and so forth—which, in essence, is the conscious self (*cidātman*)—and in causing other forms to recede;

however, it has been stated that in the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), there is nothing whatsoever to be discarded. (AbhTs 4.19) Furthermore, what is called "residence in duality" (*dvaitādhivāsa*) is not some separate, substantial entity, but rather merely the non-manifestation of one's own true nature (*svarūpākhyāti*); therefore, when it is said that the abandonment of duality is performed through conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), [it means that duality is merely a mental construct]. (AbhTs 4.20)

This ultimate reality (paramārtha), which is the self-nature manifesting as light, assumes the state of non-manifestation (akhyāti) by its own freedom; then, having gradually cast that aside, it shines forth through this sequence: being oriented toward unfolding, then unfolding, and finally fully unfolded. Such manifestation is also the very nature of the Supreme Lord; therefore, the limbs of yoga do not apply here directly.
The means (upāya).
Regarding reasoning (tarka), they may indeed support it, yet only correct reasoning (sattarka) is the direct means in that regard; and that itself is pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā).
That [knowledge] becomes refined through many modes, such as sacrifice (yāga), oblation (homa), recitation (japa), vow (vrata), and yoga. In that context:

Since the Supreme Lord alone is the locus of all entities and nothing else exists apart from Him, the sacrifice (*yāga*) is the offering of all things to the Supreme Lord for the sake of establishing the firm conviction that He is everything. With the intention that this offering to the Supreme Lord is easily accomplished by those who spontaneously partake in the penetration of consciousness because of its heart-pleasing nature, [the text speaks of] flowers, libations, perfumes, and so forth, which are dear to the heart.
The external application has been stated.

For the sake of attaining the firmly established conceptualization that "all entities consist of the splendor of the Supreme Lord," *homa* (the sacrificial oblation) is the dissolution of all entities— which is accompanied by the realization that nothing remains but that very splendor— into the fire-splendor of the consciousness of the Supreme Lord, which is intent upon the relish of devouring all entities.

Likewise, for the sake of the arising of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that consists of both [subject and object], and without depending on distinct entities such as external or internal objects of knowledge, one internally reflects that "this supreme reality (*paraṃ tattvaṃ*), which is of such a nature, is my own essential being (*svasvabhāva*). This internal reflection is *japa*. (AbhTs 4.24) For the sake of attaining the sense of identity with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-abhimāna*)—which is effortless (*nirupāya*) at all times and in all places—one views even the body or even an object like a jar with the sense of identity with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-samatā-abhimāna*). This is *vrata*. (AbhTs 4.25)
As it is stated in the *Śrīnandiśikhā*: "Supreme equality is the highest vow" (*AbhTs* 4.26).

Thus, by means of various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) which are aspects of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), that innate ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*)—which is independent of conceptual construction—is revealed. For the sake of ascending to the state of being that very [reality], which is eternally nothing but such a manifestation, there is the practice consisting of the contemplation of its own nature.
Yoga is a specific kind of conceptualization (vikalpaviśeṣa).

In this context, the Supreme Lord has the nature of perfect consciousness; his fullness itself is his power (śakti), his family (kula), his capacity (sāmarthya), his wave (ūrmi), his heart (hṛdaya), his essence (sāra), his vibration (spanda), his manifestation (vibhūti), his triad (trīśikā), Kālī, Karṣaṇī, Caṇḍī, Vāṇī, enjoyment (bhoga), vision (dṛk), the eternal (nityā), and so forth.

It is designated by various scriptural terms that function according to their respective etymologies, so that it may abide in the hearts of meditators in those various forms. And that consciousness of fullness shines forth through the manifestation of its complete power.
And his powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are innumerable. What need is there for more? Whatever constitutes the universe, those are his powers; how could they be taught?

In this regard, the universe is contained within three [powers], by which the Supreme Lord maintains, perceives, and illumines all this—from Śiva down to the earth—as being essentially nothing but non-conceptualizing pure consciousness (*avikalpya-saṃvinmātra*). That [power]...

His is the venerable *para* (supreme) power (*śakti*), by which [the world] exists through both difference and non-difference, like a reflection in a mirror or an elephant [in a dream]; she is his venerable *parāpara* (supreme-non-supreme) power.
By which [the world] exists through difference alone, with mutually distinct natures, she is his venerable *apara* (non-supreme) power.

That Blessed Lady, the venerable Śrīparā herself—also designated by other names such as Śrīmanmātṛsadbhāva and Kālakarṣiṇī—who, through the nature of synthesis, swallows these threefold [powers] by embracing them within herself, consists of these four powers which, by virtue of her absolute freedom (svātantrya), each exist in a threefold manner.
Thus, they become twelve: in emission (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), and withdrawal (saṃhāra).
For indeed, consciousness first conceives of an object within itself; then it conceives of it externally with clarity;
having grasped its state of being colored [by attachment] therein, it then conceives of that very same object with the desire to withdraw it within;
and thereafter, it both creates and swallows the doubt that acts as an obstacle to that withdrawal, having swallowed that portion of doubt.

He perceives the aspect of existence within himself through the process of withdrawal; from that, he perceives his own nature as the "agent of withdrawal," thinking, "this is my form. Then, in the perception of that nature as the agent of withdrawal, he perceives some entities as persisting in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and others as remaining as pure consciousness alone (*saṃvinmātra*). Consequently, this occurs as being inseparable from the very perception of his own essential nature.

She impels the wheel of the instruments (*karaṇacakra*); then She impels even the Lord of the Instruments (*karaṇeśvara*); then She impels even the constructed form of the subject belonging to *māyā*;
She impels the subject who delights in the grasping of expansion while being intent on the abandonment of contraction; and thus She impels even the expanded form.
These twelve divine consciousnesses [act] with reference to subjects, whether individually or collectively.

Whether existing simultaneously, sequentially, in pairs, in threes, and so forth, these [energies], participating in manifestation and revolving like a wheel, appear externally according to the sequence of months, kalās, and zodiac signs, or ultimately even as jars, cloths, and the like; nourishing the sovereignty of the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara),
they are designated by the term "Śrī Kālī."

"Calculation (*kalana*), movement (*gati*), projection (*kṣepa*), knowledge (*jñāna*), enumeration (*gaṇana*), making [objects] into objects of experience (*bhogīkaraṇa*), sounding (*śabdana*), and causing [them] to dissolve into one's own self (*svātmalayīkaraṇa*). (AbhTs 4.39) As the venerable teachers, the Bhūtirājas, have said: "Time (*kāla*) is so called because of its capacity for calculation (*kalana*), and because it projects (*kṣepāt*) and knows (*jñānāt*) by means of its power of calculation. (AbhTs 4.40) And this meaning should be examined in detail in my various commentaries, such as those on the *Prakaraṇas* and the *Stotras*. (AbhTs 4.41)
"Our teachers maintain that what is not extremely secret should not be disclosed to just anyone, yet it must not be kept hidden in every respect.
(AbhTs 4.42) Thus, whatever has been mentioned regarding sacrifice, fire-oblation, and so forth, should be understood as being directed toward Maheśvara alone in this manner.
(AbhTs 4.43) For everyone perceives everything from Viṣṇu down to Śiva—which is indeed entirely to be abandoned—as the ground of what is to be accepted, by virtue of their being the Supreme Śiva.

And since that false view must necessarily be abandoned by the practitioners of unsurpassed yoga, it is for this very purpose that there is such great zeal in the *Anubhavastotra* of the Lord of Knowledge (*Vidyādhipati*). In such a fivefold cycle consisting of sacrifice and so forth up to yoga, one should act in whatever way firm establishment occurs in each individual part through many methods; however, one should not do so by means of discriminating between what is fit to be eaten and what is not, or between purity and impurity, and the like.

It has been stated in the *Śrīpūrva* and other scriptures that one should not weary oneself with a conceptual construction whose essence is mere imagination and which is devoid of the reality of things (*vastu*).

For purity is not an inherent property of an object like its blueness; otherwise, there would be an injunction for that very same thing to be impure elsewhere—just as there is an injunction for giving [as a duty] when one is initiated.
If it is argued that "that [giving] is impure in that context," then the same applies to any other injunction; furthermore, such another injunction is non-existent.

If it is argued that [the Vedic injunction] is sublated by that [Śaiva scripture], we reply: no. It is the Śaiva injunction alone that possesses the power of sublation, as this is established by reasoning and proven by the infinite scriptures such as the *Sarvajñānottara*;
this we shall explain later.

Therefore, whether it be a rule, an injunction, or a prohibition, even if it is stated in the Vedic texts or in the scriptures of the Supreme Lord’s Siddhānta, Tantra, Kula, Ucchuṣma, and so forth, it is entirely ineffective here [in the context of the higher realization].
Thus it is established.
And likewise, that which was stated in the *Śrīpūrva* and other [Tantras] should be sought at length from the *Tantrāloka*.
*Tantrasāra*, Fifth Chapter.

In that regard, when conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) itself becomes capable of performing its own refinement within itself, independent of any other means, then— having fallen away from the activity of the bound soul (*pāśava-vyāpāra*), having attained the nature of the Supreme Lord’s power through the grace of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), and being relied upon as a means— it brings forth Śākta knowledge. (AbhTs 5.1)
And this has been determined in the immediately preceding chapter.

However, when he requires another means for the sake of his own purification, then, perceiving limited forms such as the intellect, vital breath, body, and jar as means, he attains the state of an individual soul (*aṇu*) and brings forth *āṇava* knowledge. In that regard:

Intellect consists of meditation; breath is both gross and subtle; the first is of the nature of utterance, and utterance is indeed the fivefold functions beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa); the subtle, however, is that which is denoted by the word "phoneme" (varṇa) and will be described later. The body, consisting of a specific configuration, is denoted by the word "instrument" (karaṇa). External objects such as jars and so forth, which will be mentioned as means for the worship of the jar, the sacrificial ground, and the liṅga, are also included.

In this regard, we shall first explain the meditation that is appropriate here: having meditated upon that very supreme reality— which has been described as self-luminous and inclusive of all principles— within the awakening of one's own heart, one should contemplate the union of the triad of fire, sun, and moon, which consists of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, until that great fire of Mahābhairava takes form, kindled by the wind of meditation.

One should contemplate that [consciousness] of his— which consists of the wheel (*cakra*), surrounded by the twelve flames of its former powers, and which has emerged through any one of the apertures such as the eyes— comes to rest upon the external object of perception; and by means of that resting [consciousness],

one should first fill that external [object] with the nature of the moon through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*), and then [fill it] with the nature of the sun through the process of maintenance (*sthiti*).
One should meditate on it as being illuminated, then dissolved into the form of the fire of reabsorption, and finally brought to the state of the Unsurpassed (anuttara). In this way,
that wheel becomes completely filled by the non-differentiation from all external objects.
Then, one should meditate with that wheel upon all things, even those remaining as latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as being thus created by it.

For one who meditates in this way without interruption, determining that the continuous flow of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal has as its ultimate reality nothing but one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*),
and that the ultimate reality of self-awareness is its sovereignty over creation and the rest— there is the state of Bhairava immediately.

But through practice, even the accomplishment of all desired goals and so forth [is attained]. One should meditate upon the self-luminous reality of the totality—the triad beginning with the subject—abiding within, having internalized it, in the abode of the bliss of the heart. (AbhTs 5.8–5.10)
One should meditate on that all-pervasive Lord, the master of the wheel of rays consisting of the twelve great powers,
as he emerges externally through the apertures of the voids, bringing about the states of emanation and so forth;
and one should meditate on that mandala, which has swallowed all internal and external existence, within oneself.
"Resting [in this state], the yogi should meditate; thus there shall be the manifestation of the Self.
These are the summary verses (AbhTs 5.14).
This concludes meditation (AbhTs 5.15). (AbhTs 5.16)

Therein, one desiring to utter the *prāṇa* first rests within the void of the heart itself; then, through the arising of the *prāṇa*, it moves outward; then, by filling the external with the moon of the *apāna*, one perceives the state of being the self of all (*sarvātmatā*). Thereafter, one becomes free from desire for anything else.

Then, through the arising of the *samāna*, one experiences rest in the union (*saṃghaṭṭa*). Finally, upon the emergence of the fire of the *udāna*, [one transcends] the conceptualization of subject, object, and so forth.
It devours.
When that devouring fire is extinguished and the *vyāna* breath arises, it vibrates, free from all limitations.
Thus, these states of rest beginning from the void (*śūnya*) and ending with the *vyāna* are themselves *nijānanda*, *nirānanda*, and *parānanda*.

The bliss of Brahman, the great bliss, and the bliss of consciousness—these six stages of bliss have been taught, for which there is a single unifying subject, free from rising and setting, whose ultimate nature is internal repose: the bliss of the universe (*jagadānanda*). Having reposed, either individually, in pairs, by tens, or in their entirety within these stages of upward movement, one attains that other reality of repose which is distinct from the body, the vital breath, and so forth.

One should purify conceptual thought by contemplating that very secret of the utterance of the seeds of emanation and withdrawal; and within these states of rest, there are five stages each, according to the gradations of entry.

Among them, first comes bliss (*ānanda*) from the touch of a portion of fullness; then emergence (*udbhava*), as one becomes established for a moment in bodilessness; then trembling (*kampa*), due to the loosening of identification with the body upon being seized by one's own power; and then sleep (*nidrā*), from the dissolution of outward-directedness.

In this way, when the state of the non-self has dissolved into the self, because the self consists of everything, the state of the non-self dissolves within the self; therefore, there is a whirling due to the arising of the great pervasion. These are the stages beginning with waking and ending with that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta). And these stages occur upon entering the wheels of the triangular *kanda*, the heart, the palate, and the upward-moving *kuṇḍalinī*.

Thus, we shall explain in its proper place that the three signs (*liṅga*) are: that supreme vibration (*spandana*) occurring at the rest of emission (*uccāra*) in which all objects of knowledge have dissolved; that which is the emerging object of knowledge; and that which is the fully emerged object of knowledge. Furthermore, the supreme sign here is the *Yoginīhṛdaya*.

In that regard, its primary nature is vibration, because it attains rest in the digit of emission (*visargakalā*) through the arising of the form of the couple (*yāmala*), characterized by contraction and expansion. Enough of this.
In this context, entry is non-manifestation.

Having first rested in one's own consciousness, and subsequently in the object of knowledge, one should fulfill that object of knowledge. When it is fulfilled, one rests therein and very swiftly withdraws the distinction between the subject and the object.

Then, through pervasion, these rest; together with the Void (Śūnya), they constitute the six stages of means (upāya). Prāṇa and the others, ending with Vyāna, and the entire expansion beginning with the waking state, dissolve therein. One who is established in practice here will, however, in no long time ascend into the abode of the reflective awareness of emission and withdrawal.
Thus are the intermediate verses.
(AbhTs 5.35) Thus is the pronunciation.
(AbhTs 5.36) Within this very pronunciation, the sound that vibrates and is mostly an indistinct imitation is the phoneme (*varṇa*); it [resides] in the seeds of emanation and withdrawal.

That is the primary form; through its practice, there is the attainment of supreme consciousness. For instance, when a letter beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*—whether accompanied by a vowel (*sākṣa*) or devoid of a vowel (*anakṣa*)—is uttered internally or recollected, there occurs a touch of the vibration of consciousness that is both equal and distinguished. Because it does not depend on conventional rules (*samaya*), it is complete. Even words that depend on conventional rules bring about the manifestation of their objects like a daydream, because they touch the unsurpassed consciousness; thus, the heart, throat, and lips are unified.

"One should unify the two *dvādaśāntas* and the heart"—this is the secret of the phonemes (*varṇarahasya*). (AbhTs 5.37) Some maintain that the internal phoneme, such as white, yellow, and so forth, which arises immediately after the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of internal touch, when manifested, causes one to experience consciousness (*saṃvit*).

(AbhTs 5.38) [This occurs] through the vibration of consciousness (*saṃvitspanda*) in the absence of an external object of expression, by means of the cessation of the movements of the moon and the sun. (AbhTs 5.39)
"But for whom, through the complete entry [of the breath], the seed-syllable of consciousness becomes full in the ritual of the phonemes"—
this is the internal verse (AbhTs 5.40).
This is the rule for the phonemes (AbhTs 5.41–5.42).
We shall explain the *karaṇa* (instrumental means) in the section on the manifestation of the *mudrās*.

In the *Tantrasāra*, the sixth chapter (*āhnika*), that very [means] is expressed by the term "the arrangement of the locations" (*sthānaprakalpana*). In that regard, the location is threefold: the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), the body, and the external [world].
And therein, with respect to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), this entire procedure—that path which is about to be described—is conceived as residing within the breath;

its very calculation of succession and non-succession is time (*kāla*). That [time] shines forth within the Supreme Lord alone, and its manifestation is the power (*śakti*) of the God named Kālī. However, the manifestation of that [time] through differentiation, in terms of succession and non-succession, is the function of the vital breath.

For consciousness alone grasps a form that is distinct from the objects of knowledge; and for this very reason, through its connection with limitations, it attains the state of being an object of cognition. Then, by its own sovereignty, falling upon the object with an eagerness to appropriate it, it becomes characterized primarily by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), taking the form of vital breath (*prāṇana*) and having the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). Since it fills the body with five forms, it therefore appears as if it were conscious. (Abhinavagupta, *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā-vimarśinī* 6.2)

In that regard, the path of action (*kriyādhvan*) consists of time (*kāla*) and space (*adhvan*). In the eastern and northern [directions], it is the path of space (*deśādhvan*) consisting of the variety of forms; therein, the paths of phonemes (*varṇa*), mantras, and words (*pada*) reside within the path of time because they consist of the supreme (*para*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), and gross (*sthūla*) aspects.
However, the residence of the path of space will be explained in its own proper occasion as consisting of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*pura*), and kalās.

In this context, although the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—which is woven like warp and woof throughout the body, both internal and external—is present everywhere, nevertheless, because its effort is clearly perceptible starting from the heart, it is from that very point onward that it must be investigated.

In that regard, the triad consisting of the power of the Lord (*prabhu-śakti*), the power of the self (*ātma-śakti*), and effort (*yatna*) is the cause for the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), due to the predominance of either the subordinate or the primary factor. (AbhTs 6.6) Therein, from the heart to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], the movement of the vital breath for everyone consists of thirty-six finger-breadths measured by one's own digits (*svāṅgula*), both in its outward departure and inward entry, because everyone possesses a body characterized by their own appropriate strength and effort.
(AbhTs 6.7) In that context, the entire duration of time—from the *ghaṭikā*, the lunar day (*tithi*), the month, and the year, up to the collection of years—is fully encompassed.

In this context, according to the established rule that a *caṣaka* consists of one and one-fifth finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the emergence of a *ghaṭikā* occurs; for a *ghaṭikā* consists of sixty *caṣakas*, and therefore it amounts to seventy-two finger-breadths. Now, regarding the emergence of the lunar days (*tithi*):

two and one-quarter finger-breadths are called a *tuṭi*. Four such *tuṭis* constitute a watch (*prahara*). Within that, each half-*tuṭi* is a junction (*saṃdhyā*). Thus, during the outward movement [of the breath] it is day, and during the inward movement it is night; this is the emergence of the lunar days.
Now, the arising of the month:

therein, the day is the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) and the night is the bright (śukla). Therein, the first half-ṭuṭi and the final half-ṭuṭi are rest (viśrānti), untouched by time; the fifteen intermediate ṭuṭis alone are the lunar days (tithis). Therein, light is rest.

And "ca" (and) refers to these very same day and night. Therein, the manifestation consisting of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is the day; the dissolution of the object of knowledge into the knower (*vedaka*) is the night. These two—the manifestation and its rest—possess infinite varieties due to the diversity of being long or short; however, when they are equal, that is the equinox (*viṣuvat*).

In that regard, during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the moon of the *apāna* breath bestows one by one its nourishing digits (*kalā*) upon the sun of the *prāṇa*, until on the fifteenth *tuṭi*, near the *dvādaśānta*, the moon— its flow of distinct digits exhausted— is absorbed into the sun of the *prāṇa* itself. Immediately thereafter, that half-*tuṭi* is the junction of the fortnights (*pakṣasaṃdhi*).

Of that half-tuṭi, the first half is the new moon (āmāvasya) and the second is the first day of the lunar fortnight (prātipada). When, during that first-day portion, the new-moon portion enters [the former] due to the interruption of the lunar day caused by the effort and attention of the breath-exhalation (*kāsa*), then there is an eclipse;
and therein, the Rāhu of the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*)—who is co-existent with the Soma in the form of the object of knowledge (*vedya*)—is present by its very nature.
Being incapable of dissolving [the object] and capable only of mere concealment, he drinks the lunar nectar situated in the sun.
Because it effects the non-differentiation of the triad of knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge, that auspicious time bestows fruits pertaining to the next world.
Then, as the vital breath (prāṇa) enters, the solar consciousness (cidarka), by means of each successive digit (kalā), fills the lunar apāna until the fifteenth day.

The *tuṭi*, the full moon (*pūrṇimā*), immediately thereafter the junction of the fortnight (*pakṣasaṃdhi*), and the eclipse—these are as previously described; however, this bestows results pertaining to this life. This is the arising of the month.
Now follows the arising of the year.
In that context, within the dark fortnight itself, there is the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), with a transition (*saṃkrānti*) every six finger-breadths from Capricorn to the end of Gemini.

There, for each finger-breadth, there are five lunar days (*tithi*); therein also lies the division of day and night. Thus, during the entry [of the breath], there is the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), which constitutes the sixfold transformation beginning with birth: the state of being in the womb (*garbhatva*), the desire to emerge (*udbhavecchā*), the state of wishing to emerge (*udbubhūṣutā*), the state of being about to emerge (*udbhaviṣyatvam*), the commencement of emergence (*udbhavārambhaḥ*), and the state of emerging (*udbhavattā*).
And thus, in sequence, [the worship] is performed in Capricorn and the other signs.
(AbhTs 6.22) In this very way, the practice here brings about the appropriate fruit.
(AbhTs 6.23) And here, the Rudras from Dakṣa to Pitāmaha and their Śaktis are the twelve presiding deities; such is the arising of the year. (AbhTs 6.24)

Sixty lunar days (*tithis*) per finger-width (*pratyaṅgula*)—according to this sequence, "the year [occurs] at the transition" (*saṃkrāntau varṣam*)—means that through the process of inhalation and exhalation, there is the arising of twelve years. Since there are three hundred lunar days per finger-width plus one-fifth of a finger-width for a year, and according to the calculation where the *caṣaka* was previously mentioned, there are five years at the transition; by this method, in a single period of exhalation and inhalation.

The emergence of the sixty-year cycle consists here of twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths], which is the number of lunar days (*tithi*). The number of breaths in a single day and night is exactly that much; therefore, one does not examine anything beyond the emergence of the sixty-year cycle, as it would be infinite. In this regard, one human year is a lunar day for the gods; by this sequence, twelve thousand divine years constitute a *caturyuga*.
Starting from four, three, two, and one [hundred years], there are eight junctions (saṃdhyā) by those hundreds.

Seventy-one cycles of the four yugas constitute a manvantara; fourteen manvantaras constitute a day of Brahmā. At the end of Brahmā’s day, when the three worlds have been consumed by the fire of time, and the other three worlds have been laid to sleep by smoke, all people are impelled with speed by the fire.

In Janaloka, they remain having become *pralayākala*s; but those who are awakened, such as Kūṣmāṇḍa, Hāṭakeśa, and others, sport in Mahāloka. Then, at the end of the night, the creation of Brahmā occurs.
By this measure, the lifespan of Brahmā is one hundred years.

That is a day for Viṣṇu, and his night is of equal duration; his lifespan is likewise one hundred [of those years]. (6.32–33) That is a day for Rudra, the lord of the world above that; his night is of equal duration. As before, a year consists of [those days and nights], and one hundred such years is also the limit of his life. (6.34)

In that regard, the attainment of the state of Śiva for Rudra occurs at the conclusion of that period; the limit of Rudra’s aforementioned office is one day for those who sustain the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), while the night of the hundred Rudras is of equal duration. Their lifespan is also a hundred [such days]. Upon the exhaustion of the hundred Rudras, there is the destruction of the cosmic egg.

In this manner, from the water-tattva up to the unmanifest (avyakta), this very sequence constitutes the lifespan of the Rudras. The lifespan of the former is a single day for the latter. Consequently, Brahmā and the Rudras, who hold authority over the elements beginning with water, abide within the unmanifest.
And at that time, Śrīkaṇṭhanātha is the one who withdraws [the world].
This is the intermediate dissolution (avāntarapralaya); upon its cessation, there is creation.
In that regard, even those [beings] mentioned in other scriptures are created.
That which is the lifespan of Śrīkaṇṭhanātha is a day for the Rudras dwelling in the Kañcukas; their night is of the same duration.
That which is their lifespan is a day for Gahaneśa, and his night is of the same length; and within that [night], everything dissolves into Māyā.
Again, Gahaneśa creates.
Thus, one who has an unmanifest time (avyaktakāla) should be multiplied by ten *parārdhas* and called a day of Māyā; its night is of equal duration. That indeed is the dissolution (*pralaya*).
A hundred times a *parārdha* multiplied by the time of *māyā* constitutes a day in the *aiśvara-tattva*.

Here, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) creates the universe; its night is of equal duration, wherein the breath comes to rest. Even when the breath has become tranquil within the abode of the *brahmabila*, that consciousness which remains there also possesses a temporal sequence.

That numerical count which results from multiplying the time of the *aiśvara* level by a hundred *parārdhas* is a day in the *sādāśiva* level; its night is of equal duration, and that itself is the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

When his own time has come to an end, Sadāśiva, having ascended through the Bindu, the Half-moon, and the Nirodhikā, dissolves into the Nāda; the Nāda dissolves into the Śakti-tattva, that into the Vyāpinī, and she into the Anāśrita. (AbhTs 6.50) The day of the Anāśrita is equal to a Parārdha multiplied by ten million times the duration of Śakti. (AbhTs 6.51) The Anāśrita [dissolves] into the state of Sāmanasa; that which is the Sāmanasa is equanimity (sāmya), and that is Brahman. (AbhTs 6.52)

From this state of equanimity, at a moment that is not [ordinarily] auspicious, there arises the revolution of the wheel that dissolves the expansion of all time previously described, occurring in the mere duration of a blink of an eye. One, ten, hundred, thousand, ten-thousand (*ayuta*), hundred-thousand (*lakṣa*), million (*niyuta*), ten-million (*koṭi*), hundred-million (*arbuda*), billion (*vṛnda*), ten-billion (*kharva*), hundred-billion (*nikharva*), trillion (*padma*), ten-trillion (*śaṅku*), hundred-trillion (*samudra*), final (*antya*), middle (*madhya*), and the supreme half (*parārdha*)— these eighteen [units] are successively multiplied by ten.
Thus is the method of calculation.

In this way, countless creations and dissolutions occur within a single Great Creation in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa); that [breath] occurs in consciousness; that [consciousness] occurs in the limiting adjunct (upādhi); and that occurs in pure consciousness alone. This vibration of pure consciousness itself is what is called the emergence of time.

Therefore, its manifold variety in dreams, mental constructs, and so forth, does not entail any contradiction. (AbhTs 6.56) Just as the emergence of time occurs within the *prāṇa*, so too it occurs within the *apāna* from the heart down to the root-seat (*mūlapīṭha*).

(AbhTs 6.57) And just as [the sequence] consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Anāśrita exists within the heart, throat, palate, forehead, the aperture of the cranial suture (*randhra*), and the dvādaśānta;

The six causes are likewise [located] in the *apāna* at the heart, the *kanda*, the *ānanda*, the contraction (*saṃkoca*), the expansion (*vikāsa*), and the *dvādaśānta*; these are the presiding deities over childhood, youth, old age, death, rebirth, and liberation.
Now follows the arising of time in the *samāna*:
the *samāna*, moving through the ten channels within the heart, carries the *rasas* (nutrients) and other elements equally throughout the entire body.
Moving there through the eight directions, it mimics, as it were, the movements of the lords of those directions for the perceiver.

Moving upward and downward, however, it performs the coming and going within the three channels. There, on the day of the equinox (viṣuvadina), at the time of dawn externally, it flows in the central channel (madhyamārga) for one and a quarter ghaṭikās.

Then, by the calculation of nine hundred breath-discharges (*prāṇavikṣepa*), there are five transits—left, right, left, right, left—lasting for two and a half *ghaṭikās* outside [the central channel]. (AbhTs 6.63) Then, when the five transits have occurred and fourteen *ghaṭikās* minus one quarter have elapsed, at midday during the autumnal equinox, there are nine hundred breaths in the right [channel]. (AbhTs 6.64) Furthermore, there is a set of five transits—right, left, right, left, right—with nine hundred [breaths] for each; this is likewise during the night. (AbhTs 6.65)

Thus, on the day of the equinox and during that night, there are twelve transits (saṃkrāntis) each. Consequently, when there is an increase or decrease in the days, there is an increase or decrease in the transits. In this way, during one year in which the vital wind (marut) is equalized, two years pass due to the absence of the conjunction of inhalation and exhalation.
Here too, the emergence of the twelve-year cycle and so forth is as before.
In the case of udāna, however, the movement of time—which consists of mere vibration—extends as far as the *dvādaśānta*.
Here too, the procedure is as before.
In the *vyāna* [wind], however, because it is all-pervasive, even though there is no sequential order, there is the emergence of time through its association with a subtle state of surging.
Now, the emergence of the phonemes (*varṇodaya*).

Therein, during each half-watch (*ardhaprahara*), there is the emergence of the groups of consonants (*vargodaya*). At the equinox (*viṣuvat*), this is equal: for each individual phoneme, there is an emergence of two hundred and sixteen breaths (*prāṇa*), which corresponds externally to thirty-six *caṣaka* measures. This is the emergence.
This arising of phonemes occurs without effort.

However, the arising of mantra is produced through effort; like the movement of a water-wheel or a mechanical pulley, by the power of a single continuous application, one who maintains the diverse arising of mantra day and night attains identity with the deity of the mantra.

In that regard, the number of risings is explained by the very number of breath-movements (*prāṇacāra*) in the ever-risen [state]. By the sequence beginning with "twice that" and "half of that," up to the wheel of one hundred and eight, there is a rising of two hundred [breaths]. Thus, for one who has come to rest in the nature of the movement—both gross and subtle—when the movement of the breath has ceased and the devouring of time (*kālagrāsa*) has occurred, this single, complete consciousness alone remains, overflowing with manifold powers.
It shines forth.

(AbhTs 6.76) It is precisely the difference in time that differentiates the cognitions, not a difference in the objects of cognition, as in the case of the knowledge [of someone] standing on a mountain peak. For as long as the duration of a cognition lasts, that alone constitutes a moment; and when there is a single emergence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is necessarily only one cognition. This must certainly be so.
Otherwise, a single conceptual cognition would not exist at all, because it is permeated by sequential sounds, and even a *mātrā* (measure) is sequential.
As it has been said: "Of that [syllable], the first half-short [portion] is acute.
Therefore, as long as another vibration (*spanda*) has not arisen, there is only one cognition.

Therefore, at the moment of recollecting the eighty-one words (*padasmaraṇa*), through the gateway of entering into various phenomena (*dharma*), this very single conceptualization (*vikalpa*) whose object is the Supreme Lord becomes, upon the swallowing of time, non-conceptual (*avikalpātman*) itself. Thus,

perceiving the entire path of time (*kālādhvan*) as nothing but the arising of the vital breath (*prāṇodaya*), and comprehending within that very [breath] the countless and manifold processes of emanation and withdrawal (*sṛṣṭisaṃhāra*), one recognizes the supreme sovereignty of the Self.
"He becomes truly liberated.

(AbhTs 6.81) Perceiving the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*) of the Self, whose nature is consciousness, and its form which extends there through time, along with the cycles of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal, one who is perpetually diligent attains the state of Bhairava. (AbhTs 6.82)
In the *Tantrasāra*, the Seventh Chapter:
Therein, this entire path of space (*deśādhvan*), born from the power of the manifestation of the diversity of forms, rests within consciousness;

by means of that [consciousness], it extends through the void, the intellect, the vital breath, the primary channels and their subsidiary wheels, and externally through the body, as far as the linga, the sacrificial ground, the image, and so forth.

The entire path is fully established. Having dissolved that entire path into the body, the body into the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that [breath] into the intellect (*dhī*), and that [intellect] into the void (*śūnya*), one becomes consciousness (*saṃvit*) that is intensely and perfectly full. One who knows the nature of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), perceiving consciousness as transcending those [principles] and having the form of Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva*), may experience it as consisting of the universe; otherwise, one would perceive only the portion that is an object of knowledge (*vedya*).

Thus, one might grasp someone as "other"—whether it be a presiding authority within Māyā or Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and so forth. Therefore, one must necessarily be intent on the knowledge of the *prakriyā* (the systematic process). As it has been said: "Knowledge does not have the *prakriyā* as its ultimate goal."
Therein, the earth-principle (*pṛthivītattva*) extends for a hundred *koṭis* and takes the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍagolaka*).
Within it are the fire of time (*kālāgni*), the hells, the netherworlds (*pātālāni*), the earth, heaven, and up to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*).
Outside the cosmic egg are one hundred Rudras.
And there is no limit to the number of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*).
From that element of earth (*dharātattva*), the element of water (*jalatattva*) is ten times greater;
from that, each subsequent element up to the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*) is ten times greater than the preceding one.
Namely: water, fire, air, ether, and the five subtle elements (tanmātras), along with the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) which contains the eleven organs;
from the ego-principle, the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) is a hundredfold;
from that, the principle of primordial nature (prakṛtitattva) is a thousandfold—this much is the cosmic egg of primordial nature (prakṛtyaṇḍa).
And that [universe] is as infinite as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
From the principle of *prakṛti*, the principle of *puruṣa* is divided ten thousandfold;
from the *puruṣas*, *niyati* is divided a hundred thousandfold.
From Niyati up to the end of the Kalā-tattva, each stage increases tenfold by a million;
that is to say: Niyati, Rāga, Aśuddhavidyā, Kāla, and Kalā.
From the Kalā-tattva, Māyā is ten-millionfold; this much constitutes the Egg of Māyā (māyāṇḍa).
From the principle of Māyā, Śuddhavidyā is ten times ten millionfold;
from the principle of Vidyā, the principle of Īśvara is one hundred times ten millionfold;
from the principle of Īśvara, the Sādākhya principle is one thousand times ten millionfold.
The Śakti-tattva, multiplied by the group [of five] starting from Sādākhya, is the Śakti-aṇḍa.

Because that Śakti exists pervading the entire path both internally and externally, she is called Vyāpinī. Thus, these principles (tattvas), existing as successive coverings, abide in the state where each subsequent one is the pervader and each preceding one is the pervaded.
The entire path, ending with the principle of Śakti and all its powers without exception, is pervaded by the Śiva-principle (śivatattva).
Furthermore, the Śiva-principle is immeasurable; it transcends all paths and yet pervades all paths.
Those worlds which exist within the intervals between these principles—their respective lords alone are situated here on earth.
Those who die in those abodes, they lead them to their respective destinies;
and by means of the sequence of initiation, they impel them progressively higher and higher.
(Tantrasāra, Eighth Chapter)

Regarding this world-system, which has been described as consisting of emanation (*vibhava*) and containing within itself infinite and diverse subjects and objects of experience: that which pervades it, whose nature is the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), is the form of Paramaśiva, which is like a supreme universal (*mahāsāmānyakalpa*).

However, that form which pervades only a limited number of specific divisions is a *tattva* (principle); for example, that which is called "earth" (*pṛthivī*), whose nature consists of luster, solidity, and grossness, and which pervades the entire Brahmāṇḍa presided over by the lords of the worlds beginning from Kālāgni and ending with Vīrabhadra.

In this regard, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) among these principles is demonstrated, and it is of two kinds: the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) and that of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). Among these, the ultimate causal relationship is as follows: [it belongs] to the independent one whose nature is that of the agent (*kartṛ*).

The manifestation of the Blessed One occurs through such a body, beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth, which is non-different from his own nature and yet rests within his own nature. However, the imagined relationship of cause and effect is constructed by the Supreme Lord’s will, animated by the principle of necessity (niyati), and it extends only as far as [that relationship persists].
When there is an appearance of a fixed sequence, even though there may be more [than that], it conforms to its own essential nature (svarūpa) to this extent alone;
therefore, by the will of the Yogin, a sprout arises from a seed, or a jar and so forth arise in dreams and the like.
And even in that case, the Supreme Lord’s status as the agent is not lost; thus, although unconstructed (akalpita), He remains established as the ultimate reality (pāramārthika).

For when form—which stands in the place of a wall—exists in its ultimate sense, all this that is being delineated is possible, and not otherwise; for this very reason, it is logical that the totality (*sāmagrī*) alone possesses the nature of the artisan. For that [totality] consists of the arrangement of all things and, by the power of independent consciousness, has as its own nature a specific mass of entities determined by their respective places, times, and states at the moment each individual thing is produced; for if it were otherwise, there would be a change in what is thus established.
Just as [the consciousness] increases, so too does the heterogeneity of the effect flourish in proportion.

(AbhTs 8.9) Thus, the Supreme Lord alone— whose very nature is the sovereignty of consciousness, whose body consists of all phenomenal entities, and who is the creator of jars and other things— is [the source], because the potter’s consciousness is not distinct from that [Lord], and because the potter’s body is included within the aggregate of all existing things.

If it is asked how the potter’s body can have the conceit of being an agent, [the answer is that] this too will be created by the Supreme Lord, just like the jar and other such objects. Therefore, even the doctrine of the causal complex (*sāmagrīvāda*) serves as a supporting argument for the agency of consciousness alone, which has the universe as its body.
For if I were present there, such a jar would not come into being. Thus,

when this "being an effect" is so conceived, even that multiplicity of ways in which the scriptures describe the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) among the principles (*tattvas*) is consistent— just as a scorpion may arise from cow dung, from a worm, from the will of a yogi, from a mantra, or from a medicinal herb.
In this regard, we shall demonstrate that [system] according to the perspective of our own Tantra.

Therein, it has been stated that the Supreme Lord is replete with five powers; by manifesting each of those powers as primary through His sovereignty, He abides in a fivefold manner. When consciousness (cit) is predominant, He is the Śiva-tattva; when bliss (ānanda) is predominant, the Śakti-tattva; and when will (icchā) is predominant, the Sadāśiva-tattva.
For since *icchā* (will) consists in the acceptance of the identity between knowledge and action, when the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) predominates it is the *īśvara-tattva*,
and when the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) predominates it is the *vidyā-tattva*.
In this regard, the lords of these *tattvas*— Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Ananta— are, like Brahmā, the common forms [of the principles] within the *nivṛtti* [kalā].

The five particularities (viśeṣas), which are the objects of the [five] subsequent paths, are as follows: the Śāmbhavas, the Śāktas, the Mantramaheshvaras, the Mantreshvaras, and the Mantras; this is the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan). Within this much, Śiva is the direct agent. Furthermore, on the Impure Path, Aghoreśa—whose other name is Ananta—creates it by the power of the Lord’s will for the sake of accomplishing the enjoyment of those individual souls (aṇus) whose craving for experience has been stirred up.

In this context, *lolika* is a movement whose nature is not yet full; it is a mere desire devoid of action, characterized by the fitness for future determination. Thus, it is not a separate category (*tattvāntara*) from the impurity (*mala*) of the person (*pums*).
However, the principle of attachment (*rāgatattva*) is desire delimited by action.

As for action, it is there merely action itself, whereas attachment is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), being variegated by the distinctions of action; this distinction will be explained later.

This impurity belongs to the Supreme Lord due to His will to conceal His own nature, and it is nothing other than that; moreover, even the earth and other elements possess substantiality only by virtue of being of the nature of the Supreme Lord’s will. That impurity, existing in the *vijñānākala*, is oriented toward destruction and therefore does not nourish its own effect, namely *karman*. However, in the case of the *pralayākala*, it remains in a state of full expansion; thus, *karman* reinforced by impurity results in the experience of the manifold variety of transmigratory existence.

Regarding the term "nimitta" (cause): it is rightly stated that the illustrious Lord Aghoreśa creates [the world] for the sake of accomplishing the experience of the individual souls (*aṇu*) which are permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those experiences;
for the agitation of impurity (*mala*) occurs solely through the power of the Lord’s will, since that which is insentient lacks the capacity for anything whatsoever on its own. (AbhTs 8.24)

It is said that the so-called *aṇu* (individual soul) is indeed a manifestation of both consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*). Its conscious nature is sovereignty itself, while its unconscious nature is impurity (*mala*). For him who creates, this [unconscious nature] consists of the will of the Supreme Lord; and because it manifests the insentient form residing in the objects to be created—which are eternally being produced—it is insentient. Furthermore, because it pervades all effects and so forth, it is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*).
The principle called *māyā* is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), and the power of the Supreme Lord named *māyā*, which brings about its manifestation,
is indeed distinct from it.
In this same way, the twofold nature of the principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with *dharā* must also be described.
And regarding this twofold nature, the teachers of Abhinavagupta have also stated the proof:
"Whatever appears in thought exists externally as well, as a distinct entity with a manifest form, like a jar.
Thus, since this same principle applies even to things such as the sky-flower [produced by] *māyā* and *kalā*, the logical reason is one of universal positive concomitance (*kevalānvayin*).

And those who resort to this knowledge, which consists of direct realization concerning the objects of *māyā*, *kalā*, *prakṛti*, *buddhi*, and so forth—they too are indeed perfected ones (*siddha*), truly perfected. (AbhTs 8.30) This being the case, the manifestation of the universe proceeds from the *māyā*-principle.
(AbhTs 8.31) And although that [manifestation] is indeed without succession, nevertheless, according to the view already stated, succession appears. (AbhTs 8.32)
That too is said there [in the scripture]: "The group beginning with *kalā* is divided according to each individual (*pratyātma*).

This is because its agency in producing effects and so forth is perceived as distinct for each individual. However, that group may at some point become unified by the will of the Lord (*īśvara*), like the selves of those in an assembly; in that state, this entire group beginning with *kalā* is pure (*śuddha*).

He who, by virtue of having the Supreme Lord as his object, performs his own duties in accordance with the attainment of His essential nature, does so because he stands in opposition to transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). We shall explain in the section on its manifestation how he becomes such through the descent of the power of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara-śaktipāta). The impure [individual], however, is the opposite of that.

In that regard, from Māyā arises Kalā, which joins the individual soul (aṇu)—who is in a state like deep sleep—with a slight degree of agency. She is like the swelling of the seed of transmigratory existence; although she is produced from the union of both Māyā and the individual soul, she modifies Māyā and not the unchangeable individual soul.
Thus, her nature is to be an effect of Māyā.
Thus, due to their mutual interpenetration, the distinction between the individual soul (puṃs) and primordial matter (kalā) is imperceptible.
However, for a certain Lord who is an authority over Māyā, through his grace, when all karma is exhausted, there occurs the discernment of Māyā from the Puruṣa;
by this, he remains above Māyā as a Vijñānākala, never again below Māyā. Or, [there occurs] the discernment of Kalā from the Puruṣa, by which—
He stands above *kala*.

(AbhTs 8.39) Or, by means of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, one does not transmigrate below *pradhāna*. (AbhTs 8.40) But upon the discrimination between *mala* and *puruṣa*, there is equality with Śiva. (AbhTs 8.41)
But when there is the vision of the fullness of the Person (puruṣa), there is indeed Śiva-hood itself.
Thus, it is the principle of *kalā* alone that bestows limited agency (*kiṃcitkartṛtva*),
and not agency for one who is ignorant.

Impure *vidyā*, which bestows the state of limited knowledge (*kiṃcijjñatva*), is born from *kalā*. That *vidyā* perceives the intellect (*buddhi*) and grasps the pleasure and other qualities residing therein through discrimination.
This is because the intellect, whose form is mixed with the qualities (*guṇa*), lacks the capacity for such discriminative apprehension.
Therefore, an object reflected in the intellect is discriminated by *vidyā*.

The state of being a partial agent—that is, agency restricted to only certain specific instances—culminates in this sense: that agency exists only in some cases; and in this regard, the operation of the principle of *rāga* (attachment) pertains to the specific portion concerning "only in some cases."
Nor is that [attachment] caused by a lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), because attachment is observed even in one who lacks dispassion.

(AbhTs 8.49) Furthermore, attachment is seen even toward things such as the Dharma in one who possesses dispassion. (AbhTs 8.50) And in the case of one who is satiated with food and so forth, although there is an absence of lack of dispassion, the internal passion does not depart. (AbhTs 8.51)
Furthermore, without that [Niyati], there would be the undesirable consequence that dispassion (*vairāgya*) would never arise.

(AbhTs 8.52) Time (*kāla*), while measuring the effect, also measures the agency (*kartṛtva*) delimited by it. Even though the nature of being a "limited entity" (*kvacittva*) is equal [in all cases], the operation of Niyati lies in the fact that agency belongs to this one [specific entity] alone.

(AbhTs 8.53) Even in the case of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), its operation is precisely this [Niyati]. Therefore, from Kalā alone, this group of four arises; this very [group] is [Kalā].
The consciousness of the form "I am acting while knowing something now" which resides in the body, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth, is called the bound soul (*paśu*).
This aforementioned group of six, beginning with *māyā*, is called the six coverings (*kañcuka*).
Because consciousness has been cast aside by Māyā, the *kalās* and other principles remain above it like coverings (*kañcukas*).

Thus, regarding that limited agency which is the effect of Māyā, it has been established that the *kalā*, operating upon that which is the "limited" aspect—the agenthood which is the qualificand—is the cause for the production of *vidyā* and the subsequent categories. Now, that portion which was called "limited" (*kiṃcit*) should be understood as the object of knowledge; and as long as that *kalā* [operates] within its own self toward that [object], [it remains so].

To that extent, this very [Kalā-tattva] effects the differentiation of the principle of Prakṛti—which is otherwise known as the equilibrium of its qualities (guṇasāmya) and consists of the mere generality permeated by the specific objects of experience characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion. Thus, the simultaneous creation of the dyad of the enjoyer and the enjoyed is dependent upon the Kalā-tattva. (AbhTs 8.58)
And here, it has been stated that their creation is, in reality, devoid of sequence; yet it has also been stated that there is indeed an appearance of sequence.

(AbhTs 8.59) Furthermore, a diverse sequence of knowledge, passion, and so forth is observed: some experience while feeling passion, while others feel passion while knowing, and so on. (AbhTs 8.60) Therefore, the description of a different sequence in scriptures such as the *Raurava* should be understood as not contradictory.
