(AbhTs 16.6) As long as he covers the wheel of the paths with a mass of flames, beautiful like smoke, this is the great practice called "The Net" (*jāla*), which brings about the desired life-force. (AbhTs 16.7)

By this [method], that which is to be covered goes, while under the power of another, into a state of being face-to-face at first; afterwards, if it is brought back, then everything is drawn from even the middle of the path as desired. (AbhTs 16.8) Whether for the purpose of attraction or elevation regarding a deceased person, or for one who is to be attracted while still living, this practice called *Jāla*—transmitted by the venerable Śambhunātha—is what has been taught by me.

(AbhTs 16.9) If it is asked, "How is it that even externally, in cases such as attraction, this does not occur without practice?", [the answer is: because when activity proceeds through the influence of attachment, aversion, and so forth, there is no entry into sovereign power (*aiśvarya*). (AbhTs 16.10)
Therefore, because [the soul] is constrained by necessity (*niyati*), there would indeed be a dependence on practice and so forth.
But here, such a state occurs through the immersion (*āveśa*) into the Supreme Lord, whose nature is grace.
For it is the Supreme Lord himself who bestows grace upon those to be graced by means of presiding over the body of the Guru.
And it has already been stated that its majesty is inconceivable.

Thus, the life-force (jīva), drawn by the application of the net, enters a body made of darbha grass or a nutmeg fruit and so forth; yet it does not move due to the absence of the totality of conditions such as the mind and the vital breaths (prāṇa). However, through the power of meditation upon it, it may indeed move even in such a body.
In that [image], as before, the consecrations beginning with sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) are performed, ending with the application of the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Here, by means of the supreme full oblation, the dissolution of that form made of darbha grass and so forth into the supreme light must be effected.
Thus, once it has been extracted, it attains liberation through that very full oblation, even if it was situated among the gods, in hell, as a preta, or among animals.

A human being, however, obtains knowledge, yoga, initiation, or discernment at that very moment, because he possesses a body fit for such authority; this is the procedure for the "rescue of the deceased" (mṛtoddharaṇa). Even for one who is living but out of sight, when the descent of power (śaktipāta) has occurred, this same sequence applies, with the exception of the fashioning of an image from darbha grass, the ritual construction, and the summoning of the soul (jīvākṛṣṭi).
The refinement (*saṃskāra*) of this [initiate] belongs only to that which is established by meditation alone.
And initiation (*dīkṣā*) bestows both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*).

Because one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are more powerful, and because the severance of the latent impressions for enjoyment is impossible, among many [types of] initiation, the refinement according to the Higher Teaching (*ūrdhvaśāsana*) is the stronger; the other, however, would serve for the sake of that [specific] refinement.
In the same way, even for one who has been initiated into the Paroṣa [tradition], there is the manifestation of knowledge and so forth.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter of the *Tantrasāra*.

Those who abide in the teachings ending with the *Dakṣiṇatantra* such as the Vaiṣṇava and others, or those who have taken up their vows, or those established in the supreme teaching—[for all these, the result is the same].
Even those who have not been authorized [to practice] and do not serve a guru of the lower scriptures, when they are turned upward by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) from the Supreme Lord,
for them this procedure applies: on another day, having fasted,

one should cause him to enter before the Blessed One— who has been worshipped with common mantras and informed of his condition— and there, having caused him to take the vow, one should cast it into the water.

Then he should bathe; having sprinkled [the disciple] and purified him with the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), and having led him in with his eyes blindfolded, he should perform the worship of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) with the common mantra. Then, in the fire consecrated as Śiva by means of the common mantra, he should perform the purification of the vow (*vrataśuddhi*); having performed what is called "enclosing with that mantra" (*tanmantrasampuṭa*), he should offer a hundred oblations ending in *svāhā*, saying: "I purify the expiation (*prāyaścitta*)."
Then follows the *pūrṇāhuti* with the word *vauṣaṭ* at the end.

Then, having summoned and worshipped the Lord of Vows (*Vrateśvara*), one should announce to him, "By the command of Śiva, be of no further concern for this [disciple]," and after satisfying and dismissing him, one should dismiss the fire; this is the extraction of the *liṅga*.
Then, his preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) and so forth are performed as before.
The initiation is according to one's desire.
(AbhTs 17.6) In the *Tantrasāra*, the eighteenth chapter:

One should consecrate a person who has well-practiced knowledge for the role of a practitioner (*sādhaka*) or as a teacher (*guru*). For even if he is devoid of all [other] characteristics, it is only the possessor of knowledge who is authorized for the role of a practitioner and for bestowing grace, and no other.

Even one who has been consecrated [is not exempt from transgression]. When the Guru has transferred his own authority (*svādhikāra*), even if he does not perform initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, he does not incur transgression; however, prior to that transfer, because of the binding of authority—which bestows the station of a Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśa*)—his failure to perform initiation and so forth is indeed a bondage for him. He, having been consecrated, [acts] for the sake of attaining identity with the deity of the mantra.

One should perform the vow of knowledge (*vidyāvrata*) for six months by practicing daily recitation, fire-oblations, and special worship; thereafter, having attained identification with that [deity], one becomes qualified for initiation and other rites. In this regard, one should not initiate those who are unfit, nor should one reject those who are fit. Even one who has been initiated should be tested regarding the granting of knowledge; even if their knowledge appears to be acquired through deception, once it is recognized as such, one should disregard it. And here, the worship of the deity and so forth should be performed according to the resources available for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Tantrasāra, the Nineteenth Chapter:

Now, for those established in the lower teachings—even down to their gurus—one should perform the initiation known as the "final consecration" (antyasaṃskāra) immediately upon death, solely through the application of the descent of power (śaktipāta) described in the "Extraction of the Dead" (mṛtoddhāra); likewise for those established in the higher teachings who have violated their commitments (luptasamaya) and have not performed atonement.
Thus is the command of the Supreme Lord.

(AbhTs 19.1) In that regard, whatever procedure has been taught for the extraction of the deceased must be performed entirely upon the body; the cremation of the corpse is to be performed with the *pūrṇāhuti*.

However, for the sake of establishing conviction among the ignorant, one should perform the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) accompanied by signs of efficacy through the power of ritual action, knowledge, and yoga. In that case:

Having projected the mantras onto the corpse in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), one should perform the drawing in (*ākṛṣya*) by means of the sequence of the net (*jālakrama*), as well as the acts of binding (*rodhana*), piercing (*vedhana*), and shaking (*ghaṭṭana*), through the process of the movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃcārakrama*) in the heart, throat, and forehead; in this way, the corpse trembles.

Then, having performed the union (*yojanikā*) with Supreme Śiva, one should burn it with the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) as part of the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*). For those who are pure or for others as well, there is the *śrāddha-initiation* (*śrāddhadīkṣā*) for three days, on the fourth day, every month, or every year.
One should perform [the rite] once a year.

Therein, having performed the ritual up to the end of the fire-oblation (*homa*), and having placed the food offering (*naivedya*) in one hand, one should meditate upon the Śakti of that [deity] in the form of its virility (*vīrya*), appearing as an object of enjoyment and having attained identity with the power of enjoyment residing in the bound soul (*paśu*), and then offer it to the Supreme Lord, the enjoyer. Thus it is said.

When the state of being an object of enjoyment has ceased, he becomes the husband himself. Although the purpose is fulfilled by even one of the following—funeral rites, the extraction of the deceased, the śrāddha, or initiation—nevertheless, for one who desires to enjoy the fruits, an abundance of ritual acts leads to an abundance of results; thus, he should perform them all.
Even for one who desires liberation, this [rite] serves to achieve identification with That (tanmayībhāva) through daily practice while living;

however, for the knower of reality (tattvajñānin), none of these rites—from the funeral ceremony (antyeṣṭi) to the ancestral offerings (śrāddha)—are of any use. His death is merely a festival day (parvadina) for those belonging to the lineage of his knowledge, because it fulfills a portion of consciousness; for such a lineage, the ultimate reality is solely the single consciousness.
Like the succession of days for one who lives and attains knowledge;

and in all these rites, such as those concerning faith (*śraddhā*), the sacrifice to the image (*mūrtiyāga*) is the primary element—this is the teaching of the venerable *Siddhāmata*, and its procedure will be explained in the *Naimittikaprakāśana*.
(Tantrasāra, Twentieth Chapter)

In that regard, there is the initiation for the sake of accomplishing the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for those fit for knowledge, and for those incapable of that, the initiation with seed (*sabījā-dīkṣā*) which bestows liberation. Once that has been performed, the Guru should instruct [the disciple] regarding the conduct for the remainder of life (*ājīva-śeṣavartana*).

Therein, the conduct for the remainder is threefold: obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*); and the last of these pertains only to the practitioner (*sādhaka*), as it need not be determined here.

In this context, that which is constant (*nitya*) is the state of being absorbed in that [reality] (*tanmayībhāva*), while the occasional (*naimittika*) consists of the performance of daily rites such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), the observance of festival days (*parvadina*), the sacred thread ceremony (*pavitraka*), and so forth. Some maintain that even these are "constant" because they are fixed to their own specific times. Others, however, hold that the occasional is not fixed even for those established in the teaching; for example, the arrival of the Guru or his circle, the day of a particular festival, the day of attaining knowledge, and the like.

In that regard, the obligatory worship consists of: the regular daily worship (*saṃdhyopāsā*), the worship of the Guru, the worship on festival days (*parvapūjā*), and the *pavitraka* rite; these must necessarily be performed.

(AbhTs 20.6) The occasional (*naimittika*) worship includes: the acquisition of knowledge, the acquisition of scriptures, the arrival at the house of the Guru or his associates, the days of their birth, consecration, and death, worldly festivals, the exposition of the scriptures, the beginning, middle, and end [of such expositions], the vision of the deity, the assembly (*melaka*), a command in a dream, and the attainment of purification from transgressions of the observances (*samaya*).
Thus, this is the specific cause for occasional worship.

In that regard, one should impart the principal mantra—endowed with vitality, having the essence of the vibration of consciousness, and unwritten—to the disciple who has received initiation, solely through the oral tradition (*vaktrāgama*). Then, for the sake of achieving identification with that [mantra], that disciple, during the junctions of the day (*saṃdhyā*), [should perform the practice].
One should practice the cultivation of identification with That (tanmayībhāva) at all times by means of that [visualization], for the sake of attaining such latent impressions (saṃskāra);
and daily, one should worship the Supreme Lord on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or in a linga.
Therein, upon a pleasing sacrificial mound meditated upon as being like a stainless mirror, one's own very form is non-different from the circle of deities to be worshipped.

Having seen [the deity] as if reflected in a physical image, one should worship it with offerings of flowers, incense, water for sipping, food, incense, lamps, hymns, songs, instrumental music, dance, and so forth; one should recite mantras and offer praise in order to attain, without hesitation, the state of being absorbed in that [deity]. For when one gazes incessantly at one’s own face in a mirror, the ascertainment of its true nature occurs very quickly; and in this matter, no other sequence is primary than the state of being absorbed in that [nature].

Our teachers maintain that for one who is permeated by identification with the supreme mantra, whose stain of animalistic tendencies has been removed, and whose entire web of bonds has been dissolved by the infusion of the flavor of devotion—that which dwells within his heart is indeed the supreme object to be attained. (AbhTs 20.11) That ultimate state of being, having taken its seat, shines forth as the expansion of consciousness. (AbhTs 20.12)

Those who know the secret worship You, the vision of supreme nectar, with that [flower]. (AbhTs 20.13) Having made the ground of the *ādhāra* washed by the momentary sprinkling of the essence of wonder, and having taken from the mind its own natural flowers which abound in their own fragrance, (AbhTs 20.14) I worship You, together with the Goddess, day and night in the temple of the body, by means of the priceless *argha*-vessel of my own heart, which is overflowing with the nectar of bliss. (AbhTs 20.15)
Contemplating the meaning expressed in these two verses, one should visualize the maṇḍala of deities.
Then follows the display of mudrās, the recitation [of mantras], and the offering to them;
finally, the dismissal by means of identity with awakening.

One should eat the principal *naivedya* oneself, or throw it all into water; for those who know the *Āgamas* maintain that aquatic creatures have been previously initiated by means of the consumption of the *caru*. However, if there is a suspicion that a cat, a mouse, a dog, or the like has eaten it, even a man of knowledge—out of a desire to favor the world—should not act in such a way [as to consume it], nor should he remain having abandoned the world; thus concludes the sacrifice on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍilayāga*).

Now, regarding the *liṅga*, one should not install a *liṅga* there with secret mantras, especially if it is a manifest (*vyakta*) one; however, in the case of those already installed, one should perform worship according to the sequence of invocation and dismissal. Therein, the *liṅga* may be the body of the Guru, one's own body, the body of the Śakti, a book of the secret scriptures, a hero’s vessel (*vīrapātra*), a rosary, a weapon, a bow, a pearl, gold, or a mirror made from pleasing substances such as flowers, perfumes, and other materials, serving as the support.
One should worship [them].

And in that regard, it is precisely through the power of the support (*ādhāra*) that there occurs an increasingly superior accomplishment of the mantra; thus, the teachers of the scriptures maintain that each preceding element is primary, because mantras conform to the qualities of their support, and therefore, for each respective goal, that particular [support] is primary.

Everywhere, the supreme refinement consists precisely in the conceit of non-difference from the Supreme Lord. Now follows the rule for the festivals (*parvan*): therein, the festival is sixfold—namely, the general, the general-general, the general-particular, the particular-general, the particular, and the particular-particular.
Because of the fulfillment of the injunction:

"In that regard, month by month, the first and fifth days are common; the fourth, eighth, ninth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both fortnights are common-to-the-common. In these two zodiac signs, there is a conjunction with the specific planets and lunar mansions appropriate for each respective lunar day, as will be described."

The general rule is as follows: the first part of the night of Mārgaśīrṣa is on the ninth day of the dark fortnight; the middle of the night of Pauṣa is on the ninth day of the dark fortnight; the middle of the night of Māgha is on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight; the middle of the day of Phālguna is on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight;

[the middle of the day] of Caitra is on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight; [the middle of the day] of Vaiśākha is on the eighth day of the dark fortnight; [the middle of the day] of Jyaiṣṭha is on the ninth day of the dark fortnight; [and so on] for Āṣāḍha.

The first day of Śrāvaṇa, the forenoon of the eleventh day of the dark fortnight; the midday of Bhādrapada, the sixth day of the bright fortnight; the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja; and the first part of the night of Kārttika, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight—these are the special festival days (viśeṣaparva).

Citrā and the Moon; Maghā and Jupiter; Tiṣya (Puṣya) and the Moon; Pūrvaphalgunī and Mercury; Śravaṇa and Mercury; Śatabhiṣaj and the Moon; Diti (Pūrvabhādrapadā) and Venus; Rohiṇī and Venus; Viśākhā and Jupiter; and Śravaṇa and the Moon—thus [is the sequence].
If this occurs in the order of the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa according to their respective numbers, excluding Āśvayuja, then there is a particularly distinguished result.

If there is a specific [feature] on another lunar day (*parvan*), they call that "anuparva. Furthermore, in the conjunction of a lunar mansion (*bha*) and a planet (*graha*), the specific time (*velā*) is not the primary factor, because the distinction is obtained from the lunar day (*tithi*) itself. However, the persistence of the time for the subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāga*) on the day of the *parvan* is primary, due to the predominance of the subsequent sacrifice. "Subsequent sacrifice" (*anuyāga*), "form-sacrifice" (*mūrtiyāga*), and "wheel-sacrifice" (*cakrayāga*) are synonyms.

In that regard, the Guru, one belonging to his lineage, along with his spiritual descendants, a knower of reality, a maiden, a low-caste woman, a courtesan, or a reddish-brown woman who knows reality—these are the primary objects of worship in the *cakrayāga*, especially when all are present together.

Therein, in the center sits the Guru; then, according to the sequence of the surrounding enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), from the Guru down to the initiate (*samayin*), in the order of Hero (*vīra*) and Power (*śakti*), or according to the arrangement of the circle or the arrangement in rows. Then, [he should worship] in due order with perfumes, incense, flowers, and so forth.

Then, one should worship the vessel by meditating upon it as the form of Sadāśiva; having filled it with liquor (āsava) conceived as the nectar of Śakti, one should worship the consuming Śakti therein as Śiva. Having performed the satiation of the circle of deities (*devatācakra*) by means of that very [liquor], and having meditated upon the union of the triad consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva, one should perform the external and internal satiation according to the sequence of the descent of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), prioritizing either liberation (*mokṣa*) or enjoyment (*bhoga*).
Furthermore, by the sequence of re-absorption, it nourishes the wheel of rotation thus completed.

Therein, having placed the vessel consisting of the universe upon the support and having gratified the circle of deities, one should gratify oneself with that which has been offered in salutation. In the absence of a vessel, the auspicious curved shell or the hand, shaped like a vessel and held auspiciously by the right hand, [should be used].

With two [hands] raised above and joined at the right, forming a curved shell (*vellita-śukti*), the Vetālas and Guhyakas are satisfied by the falling drops, while Bhairava is satisfied by the continuous stream. No one should be allowed entry here;
if anyone enters through negligence, one should not perform an investigation, but rather perform the wheel-sacrifice (*cakrayāga*) twice over. Then, [offer] the appetizers (*avadaṃśa*).

One should scatter food and other offerings at will in front [of the deities] or within a secret chamber, excluding the use of conventional names; rather, one should unite all [the guests] by means of the word "deity. This is the *vīrasaṃkarayāga*. Then, at the conclusion, one should satisfy them with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), betel, clothing, and so forth. This is the most preeminent *mūrtiyāga*.

Even one who has not seen the maṇḍala, by worshipping on the festival days through the sacrifice of the form (mūrtiyāga), attains within a year alone the fruit spoken of for a "son" (putraka), even without the performance of the twilight rites and so forth; this is the rule for elders, enjoyers, and women, which should be taught by the Guru when there is a descent of power (śaktipāta). AbhTs 20.38.

Now follows the procedure for the *pavitraka* (the sacred thread). This [procedure], performed according to the rules as taught in the *Śrīratnamālā*, the *Triśiromata*, the *Śrīsiddhāmata*, and other scriptures, fulfills the command of the Supreme Lord (*Pārameśvara*). And this has been stated in the *Śrītantrāloka*: "Without the *pavitraka*, everything is fruitless."

In that regard, the *pavitraka* rite is to be performed from the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha until the full moon of the *kula* [fortnight]; therein, on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, the *kulacakra* fulfills the *nityācakra*, according to those who know the *Śrīnityātantra*.

On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, according to those who know the *Śrībhairavakulormi*. On the fifteenth day at the end of the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), according to those who know the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*.

There, having worshipped the deity with offerings according to one's means and having gratified him with oblations, one should present a *pavitraka* (purifying thread). It may be fashioned from gold, pearls, and gems, down to those made of cloth, cotton thread, or containing *kuśa* grass.
That [thread] should have knots numbering the total of the *tattvas*, as well as knots numbering the *padas*, *kalās*, *bhuvanas*, *varṇas*, and *mantras*, and it should reach down to the knees.

One [strand] should end at the navel, another at the throat, another on the head, and another [on the forehead]; thus one should offer four purifiers (*pavitraka*) to the deity and the guru, while meditating upon their form as being complete with all the paths (*adhvan*), and give one to the remaining [deities]. Then a great festival (*mahotsava*) should be performed for four months, seven days, or three days; these are the primary and secondary ritual options.

When wealth is available, one should perform the *pavitraka* rite every month, or else every four months, or even once a year; if it is not performed, one should recite the mantra as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Even a wise man, even if he possesses the means, incurs sin by failing to do so, for if he fails due to being overcome by greed, he falls into the reproach of disparaging knowledge.
"Even when one has attained realization, if the teaching of the Supreme Lord is defiled, then one must perform penance"—
from this statement [it follows].
Thus ends the procedure for the *pavitraka* rite.

In all cases— whether at the attainment of knowledge and so forth, or even at the conclusion of a worldly festival— there is an intensification of the radiance of consciousness and the presence of the circle of deities (devatācakra). Therefore, by reflecting upon such an intensification, one should perform the corresponding specific rite during the secondary sacrifice (anuyāga) and other such occasions.
Now, the procedure for exposition (vyākhyāvidhi).

(AbhTs 20.51) One should request a teacher who is fully accomplished in all the scriptures for the purpose of exposition. He, in turn, should expound the scripture—provided it is suitable for the disciple’s specific refinement—to his own disciple or even to the disciple of another; for even toward one who stands within a lower teaching, he may do so out of compassion, his heart being moved by the possibility of a descent of power (śaktipāta) manifested through the variety of the Lord’s will.

One should explain [the text], with the exception of the instruction on the vital points (*marman*). In that regard, the exposition becomes fruitful when given to those who are seated on low seats, who are intent upon it, and whose speech, mind, and body are restrained; first, having either drawn or mentally visualized a lotus-base on the ground smeared with perfumes and other substances.
One should worship a square mandala with three lotuses; in the center of the lotus, Vāgīśī, and on the left and right, Gaṇapati and the Guru.

In the foundational lotus (ādhārapadma), one should worship the deity of the Kalpa to be explained. Then, by means of the application of the common arghya vessel, one should satisfy the maṇḍala, and thereafter one should expound the aphorisms, sentences, chapters, and texts.

Acting in a manner that is not contradictory between what precedes and what follows, and in accordance with the logical propriety of the treatises—such as *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, *prasaṅga*, *samuccaya*, and *vikalpa*—one should explain up to the end of the chapter, neither more nor less: first properly formulating the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), then properly refuting it, establishing the thesis (*sādhya*), and demonstrating the intended meaning (*tātparya-vṛtti*). Furthermore, at the conclusion of each subject matter (*vastu*), there should be an offering of libations (*tarpaṇa*) and worship (*pūjana*).

Thus [it continues] until the completion of the commentary. (AbhTs 20.54) Then, having worshipped the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) and dismissed it, one should smear [the ground] and cast it into the deep.
(AbhTs 20.55) This is the procedure for the commentary. (AbhTs 20.56)

Now, the expiation for transgressions of the rules (*samayaniṣkṛti*). Although there is no need for penance or the like for one who is established in the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), nevertheless, in order to favor those who partake in liberation solely through the practice (*caryā*), one should demonstrate the path of conduct. However, for one who does not know reality, whose enjoyment and liberation depend entirely upon the practice, if a transgression of the rules has been committed and he fails to perform penance—

"One becomes a flesh-eater for a hundred years"—this is the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) that must be stated there; however, in the case of killing a woman, there is no expiation. In other cases, having understood the relative strength [of the offense], one should repeat the *Mālinī* of the Blessed One (*Bhagavatī*) in its unbroken form from one time up to three hundred thousand times, until doubt is dispelled. At the conclusion of that, there is a special worship, and therein also the *Cakrayāga*; for that indeed [is the remedy].
"In all cases, he is the remainder" (AbhTs_20.59).
Thus ends the rule for the atonement of the commitments (samaya).
Now follows the rule for the worship of the Guru (AbhTs_20.61).

At the conclusion of all sacrifices, once the sacrifice has been completed, one should perform the worship of the Guru on the following day. For previously he was gratified as a subordinate member of the ritual procedure, but not as the primary object; therefore, by failing to perform that worship with primacy, one becomes bound by the fetter of the [ritual] entitlement.
Thus, one should perform it in every way.

There, having drawn a svastika mandala and placed a golden seat upon it, one should worship the entire path therein, consecrate that seat with it, and perform worship for it. Having offered libations, food, a sacrificial fee, and oneself, and having requested the remnants of the food offering and paid obeisance, one should consume them oneself and then perform the worship of the wheel.
Thus ends the procedure for the worship of the Guru. The entire daily and occasional ritual has been described in this way.
Now, the authority of this very scripture is being stated:

therein, since the universe consists of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), and since consciousness is of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and since reflective awareness is established as being of the nature of verbalization (*śabdana*), [the authority follows] regarding the objects residing in the entire world and the variety of the relationship between actions and their fruits pertaining to them.

That which is reflective discernment (*vimarśana*) is itself the scripture; thus, the entire collection of scriptures is in reality non-different from the very nature of the Supreme Lord, leading to a single fruit for a single qualified seeker. However, it is solely through the power of the Supreme Lord’s will (*niyati-śakti*) that these [teachings] become established among people in distinct, partial forms. 21.3.

Some are established in the Vedas, Āgamas, and other scriptures, which consist of the conceptualization of distinctions appropriate to *māyā*; others, with the conceit of liberation, are likewise situated in the Sāṃkhya, Vaiṣṇava, and other such scriptures; yet others are in the Śaiva Siddhānta and similar systems, whose essence is the contemplation of the nature of Śiva as distinct [from the world]; still others are in the *Mataṅga* and other scriptures, whose essence is the contemplation of the Supreme Lord as consisting of all things; while some, though extremely rare, are established in the contemplation of the essential nature of the Supreme Lord, who consists of consciousness and whose ultimate reality is the bliss of absolute freedom, devoid of all limitations.

In the sequence of the Śrī Trika scriptures, however, some maintain that the accomplishment of a single fruit occurs from a single scripture alone, either by abandoning each preceding one in succession or by skipping them.
Even in the doctrine of duality, since all scriptures have their origin in the activity of a single Lord, their authority remains established, for the basis of authority [is the same].

Since partial agreement, lack of contradiction, and the absence of non-occurrence are equal [in both cases], mutual sublation is ineffective because their objects differ. This is like the case of the killing of a Brahmin and its prohibition; there is a difference in the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and an excellence of those rites, while in the absence of that [excellence], there is in some cases a lack of qualification [for the act].

Thus, it is the same as in the case of the different stages of life (*āśrama*): there is an excellence [of authority] due to the excellence of the fruit. Even though the Upaniṣadic portions therein have different authors, it is possible here that they were composed by an omniscient being, because they are joined with logical arguments stated by him and with matters beyond those [ordinary means]. Furthermore, even if the scriptures (*āgama*) are eternal, their established status must necessarily be accepted, since their validity depends upon perception (*adhyakṣa*), inference through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and other such means.

Because it is rooted in that [perception], the statement "I see real silver" is indeed an *āgama* (scriptural authority) consisting of the very well-known consensus of others, such as goldsmiths; this [consensus] has some visible fruit, for even a child's activity in various instances— such as "the hungry person eats"— proceeds solely from such common knowledge,
and not from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because those two are absent at that time, though they may exist during the stage of youth.

Even that [notion] is ineffective; however, taking public renown as its foundation, let it serve some purpose for someone. One [form of renown] yields the fruit of liberation (*kaivalya*) for a person who has not seen Vaidehī or whose nature has dissolved;
another yields the fruit of equality with Śiva; and another culminates in identity. And each of these is of many kinds.
Thus, in this world filled with manifold renown, whatever kind of person one is destined to become, one will attain renown of just such a kind.
"One considers [the scripture] to reside in the heart precisely by force.

Thus, for a person who is empty [of such realization], this formulation of words is excessive; however, by one who validates some degree of their renown as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the authority of scripture (*āgama-prāmāṇya*) must indeed be accepted. Therefore, that scripture should be resorted to in which the supreme fruit is found—enough of this further discussion.

Since [the world] shines exactly as it is perceived by virtue of being the ultimate reality of the light of consciousness, and since the wise likewise perceive it in that very way, you— discerning this— should take refuge in the scripture whose essence is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the manifestation of the all-encompassing Consciousness, which is the unsurpassed Self. In whatever worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is firmly established through its own perfection, in that very thing I am without doubt.
"Be such that, through the firm establishment of your own conviction, you become Supreme Śiva.
(AbhTs 21.11) When worldly activity is fashioned from one's own firm conviction, people proceed without hesitation.
(AbhTs 21.12) Then one becomes Supreme Śiva, established in a conviction that has transcended the common folk. (AbhTs 21.13)
The Essence of Tantra, the Twenty-second Chapter.
Now, this entire mode of worship is described according to the venerable Kaulika method for those qualified aspirants in whom such firm latent impressions have fully awakened.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Yogasaṃcāra* and other texts: "Brahman is bliss; it resides in that body in a threefold manner at the end of the eight. (AbhTs 22.1)
Because of abandoning that [practice], those who do not practice celibacy are deprived of bliss;
the sacrificers of the Cakra, excluding the artificial food of bliss, [fall likewise].
Both [groups] go to a terrible hell; therefore, one should adhere to this state.
Thus, by this arrangement, the *kulayāga* is sixfold: externally, in the *śakti*, in one's own body, in the couple (*yāmala*), in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and in consciousness (*saṃvit*).
Among these, each subsequent one is superior and each preceding one is inferior for the sake of preference.

For one who desires supernatural powers (*siddhi*), the second, fourth, and fifth must be performed in every way; however, for one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*), the sixth is primary. Even for such a seeker, the second and the others must indeed be practiced as occasion arises.
And for the sake of fulfilling the ritual injunctions:

there, the external sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) is filled with bliss; the vessel for the heroes (*vīrapātra*), a reddish cloth, or even the previously mentioned *liṅga* and so forth [are used]. Therein, without regard for the necessity of performing rituals such as bathing, one first attains purity solely through resting in full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*).

Having meditated upon the unification of the vital breath, consciousness, and the body— and because consciousness is of the nature of Paramaśiva— one should recite the mantra twenty-seven times over the head, face, heart, secret place, and the physical form, both in direct and reverse order, so that the entire path (*viśvādhvan*) may be fulfilled within the Supreme Lord,
whether in His state of non-supremacy (*aparatva*), His intermediate state (*parāparatva*), or His supreme state (*paratva*).

For instance, the twenty-seven principles (tattvas), beginning with Māyā, Puruṣa, Prakṛti, the Guṇas, and Buddhi, and ending with Earth, are included therein because the Kalās and so forth are subsumed within them; likewise, even regarding the higher and lower aspects of the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti), the venerable Lakuleśvarapāda and others have stated that the five Brahmans— Sadyojāta, Ājāta, Bhava, Udbhava, and so on— are themselves of the nature of these twenty-seven forms.

Even in its state as the "other" (paratva), the Supreme Lord possesses five powers, and each power likewise has five forms; thus there are twenty-five powers. These are mutually undivided, such that they constitute a single power, and that [single power] is itself undivided.
By means of this pervasion consisting of twenty-seven forms, one [attains] the flame of the fire of consciousness—the form of intellect and vital breath—merely by a single utterance.
One should perform the "binding" (*baddhā*) by which Supreme Śiva alone is bound, so that nothing whatsoever transcending the Tantra may run away;

through the piercing of the wheel of the instruments (*karaṇacakra*) presided over by such an intellect, one should make even the sacrificial substances, the house, the directions, the substratum, and so forth, present before one, become identical with Him.
Then, one should fill and worship the vessel of honor (*arghapātra*) precisely through the pervasion of the binding of the crest-lock (*śikhābandha*).

And with the droplets from that [liquid] and with its essence, by means of the union of the left ring finger and the thumb, one should worship and satiate the mantra-circle within the wheels of the body; thereafter, until the end of the breath, one should fashion a seat consisting of a trident ending in the three powers (śaktis) upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila). Indeed, in the case of the *sārṇa* [mantra], one should fashion the seat ending in the letter *au*, which concludes with *māyā* and the three powers.

Indeed, having performed the deposition of the container and the contained by pronouncing just once the syllable *hi* along with the vowel *au*— which ends with the three powers— and above that the *yājyā*, which is the power whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), one should perceive the universe within that very consciousness which serves as the container.
And since even that [universe] consists of consciousness, there occurs a mutual encapsulation (*sampuṭībhāva*) of the universe by consciousness and of that [consciousness] by the universe.

Since the universe arises from consciousness and culminates in that very same [consciousness], and since consciousness arises from the object of knowledge and rests in that very same [object], the reality of consciousness is obtained through these two forms of encapsulation (*saṃpuṭībhāva*).
Thus it has been said: "But having encapsulated the emission (*sṛṣṭi*)."

Then, having offered everything from perfumes, incense, and fragrant flowers up to the state of one's own total prostration, and having performed the recitation (*japa*) while resting in one's own nature, one should withdraw [the visualization] and cast it into the water.
Thus ends the external sacrifice (*bāhyayāga*).

Now, regarding the power (*śakti*): therein, through the mutual manifestation of the *śaktis*, the *tālas*, and the *sāvikas*—that is, of both [male and female practitioners] as being of a dual nature—there occurs the awakening of Śiva and Śakti at the beginning and end of the creation of the outpouring (*prollāsa*).

Due to their mutual interaction and by the necessity of the Supreme Lord, they possess primacy there in their pure form; by this, the nature of the specific wheel (*viśiṣṭacakra*) as power (*śaktitva*) is also explained. In that regard, the worship consists solely in the pervasion of the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandha*), extending up to the three powers. The specific distinction in the pervasion is that the seat (*āsana*) is in the three corners, while the power of emission (*visargaśakti*) is in the center.
Thus, within one's own body, [the union occurs] first in that very *cakra*, and then in the secondary *cakras* beginning with the *brahmarandhra*.
Now, this is the characteristic of the *yāmala* (union) of Śakti; likewise, there is non-differentiation (*abheda*).
Therefore, disregarding age, caste, and so forth, due to non-attachment, there is indeed identity (*tādātmya*) born from a pair that transcends the world.
Because they arise as effect, cause, or simultaneously, they are threefold—

either directly or otherwise. Therefore, having worshipped them mutually, one should satisfy them by means of bliss up to the end, and then worship the *cakra* according to its propriety, as well as the subordinate *anucakra* that follows it.
Externally by means of flowers and the like, and internally by means of perfumes, food, liquor,
and so forth; thus, with its state overflowing through activities that produce a mass of bliss,
the host of the subordinate wheels merges into identity with the [central] wheel.
In the reflective awareness of their own essential nature, which consists of the unfolding expansion of their respective enjoyments,
the goddesses of the subordinate wheels gradually enter the central wheel of consciousness.
Having attained vigor through the fulfillment of the multitude of rays whose essence is the deities of the subordinate wheels, [they proceed].
That [pair], consisting of power and the possessor of power, becomes mutually oriented toward one another.
That pair, through the agitation born from the vibration of entering the upper abode, agitates the subordinate wheels as well;
at that time, they are identical with it and not separate.
When this couple (yāmala) has thus become free from all discourse regarding duality,
then, through the application of the gradations of the sequence, that very consciousness is the union of emission (visarga).
That is the supreme abode of the eternal, the noble bliss consisting of both [subject and object], the universe itself.
Neither quiescent nor arisen, the supreme Kaula is the cause of the birth of both the quiescent and the arisen.
One who desires the uninterrupted state should assimilate that consciousness as one's own.
Then, the duality consisting of the quiescent and the arisen arises simultaneously for both power and the possessor of power.

Due to the mutual penetration of their own selves, when the two are stilled, they possess the nature of both; yet it is Power (Śakti), arising in that manner, who nourishes the emanation, not the possessor of power (tadvān). And within that [Power] resides the noble Kula; furthermore, through her, the conjunction of the aforementioned yoga occurs among men.
Now, in this twofold creation consisting of the quiescent and the emergent states,
those who contemplate [the reality] are established in the undivided plane where the existence of emission resides in the primordial [state].
And that which has emerged is grasped externally from one primary mouth to another through mutual interaction.
When the circle of goddesses is satisfied, it bestows the accomplishments, gnosis, and liberation.
Through the practice of tranquility, that circle of deities here attains peaceful Śiva;
it is empty, consisting of supreme bliss, and is the worthy object of worship from the state of one's own natural nirvāṇa.

Through the savor of relishing external objects filled with its own essence—which possesses the flavor of longing—that wheel [of the senses] moves along with the inner, full, and surging secondary wheels; then that [central] wheel also surges forth as before. Thus, this emission (*visarga*) is threefold, according to its literal meaning.

In this lotus, which has the ever-arisen Maṅgala as its covering and rests within the three corners, the mantra— consisting of the semen-virility (*vīrya*) of Manu in its threefold form through the act of touching the abode of emission (*visarga*)— and containing that respective consciousness, brings forth the corresponding fruit.
The root of the excellent sixteen-petaled lotus is not capable [of functioning] if it is eternally separated from its stalk.
Through the process of the friction of the pair of lotuses strung upon the central stalk,
and through the collision of the mass of rays of the sun with the moon-like beauty situated in the center, [the fire arises] in the southeast.
Through the union of the three-petaled [lotus] with the red energy (*vīryakalā*), there is the production of the sprout in the center; thus,
by the seal of the conjunction of the Moon,
the Sun, and Fire, one who brings the sequence of emanation and so forth to an end within attains stability in the Fourth State (*turya*).
This [state] occurs during the penetration of the Khecara-mudrā through the mutual union of the Śakti and the possessor of Śakti;
it consists of reflective awareness (vimarśamaya) found in drinking, enjoyment, play, laughter, and so forth,
manifesting as unmanifest sound, resonance, roar, explosion, audible sound, resonance, and the end of resonance.
That is the potency of mantra through the uninterrupted, unstruck ultimate reality (anāhata-paramārtha) during the phases of going,
coming, and resting; in the contact with the two targets at the ear and the eye,
in the yoga of their closing, and in the twin wheel (yamala-cakra) known as the end of the body.

That which is unmanifest, located in the throat from the region of the heart between the breasts down to the edge of the lips, is situated between the two wheels; having heard it at the moment the agitation subsides, they attain extinction therein. And thus, that which is the supreme eightfold Bhairava of Sound (nāda) [is present].
Because light and sound [arise] from that, it is called the supreme mantra-pervasion;
for the wise one who lives [in this state], there shall be liberation in every action.
One who knows that is liberated in the scripture, a vessel for the higher-kula realization, and the [true] embryo.
One should make the abode both empty and non-empty; within the single staff, fire and wind are brought to a state of equal flavor, like one taste within taste.
Free from apprehension and beyond conventional conduct, one should contemplate: "I am not."
Seeing the deities residing within the body in the mass of consciousness as joy, agitation, and so forth,
and constantly seeing the host of deities situated in the circles of the ears, eyes, mouth, nose, and other [senses] as the perceiver, one certainly attains success through the Khecarī [mudrā].
"Quickly casting one's own body into a very deep abyss,
one should practice this 'Sky-farer' mudrā by looking while contracting both hands with non-violence.
Thus is this Yāmalayāga.

When the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is of the nature of the universe and possesses the aforementioned pervasiveness, is strengthened by the offering of food, fragrance, incense, and so forth—accompanied by the previously described pervasion of consciousness (*saṃvit*)—this is the *prāṇayāga* (sacrifice of the vital breath). However, the *saṃvidyāga* (sacrifice of consciousness), which consists of the ascent into rest within consciousness, has already been explained [previously].
Thus, having performed one of these sacrifices, if one’s heart is adorned with such unwavering certainty...

When he becomes a disciple, then, having first shown him that sacrifice, one should perform initiation for him through observation according to the previously stated pervasion and the sequence of contemplation, without even requiring oblations of sesame and clarified butter; however, in the case of initiation in absentia and other occasional rites,
the procedure is exactly as before.
This [is said] solely because this sacrifice is the primary one.

In the body of the Guru, the seventh Kulayāga is the most excellent of all; even that, when performed just once in conjunction with the previous sacrifices, fulfills everything. May there be auspiciousness!
